Paulo Murillo tells his husband Kevin Chase about the sign that stood as a beacon of hope over West Hollywood when he arrived there as a young man at the height of the AIDS crisis.

This conversation was recorded as part of a partnership between StoryCorps Studios and the City of West Hollywood.

Learn more: https://storycorps.org/stories/a-sign-to-safe-haven-in-west-hollywood-during-the-aids-crisis/
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en My father was a gardener. So I would go with my dad as a kid in a truck, you know, mowing lawns. My father had the same route for decades up and down Santa Monica Boulevard. And there was a sign, a West Hollywood sign. I would see that sign and I would see gay men, you know, attractive men holding hands. So I would always look for that sign. One day we were driving and I saw the sign and I perked up and I was looking around and a guy looked at me and he blew a kiss at me. >> Well, you're with your dad. >> Yes. >> How'd that go down? >> I never saw that son again. He never drove past Santa Monica Boulevard again. By then I was already playing with Barbie dolls and you know a different weird kid or whatever. And I would have fantasies of running away to the city where gay people lived and were not afraid to be out on the street holding hands. I came out of the closet fresh out of high school and my mom when she found out I was gay, she's like, "Pack your stuff. You have to go. You can't be in this house. I'm not going to have you humiliate this family. I didn't talk to my parents for a year." >> You left home at what 18, 19. >> Yeah. But I just wasn't ready to be on my own. And I was like, I need to find that sign that I used to see when I was a kid. It was a symbol of gayness. It was a symbol of safness. >> It was a touchstone. >> Yeah. >> So coming out in 1991, a lot of people had died of AIDS. There was just a lot of fear and a lot of stigma. But that sign was the symbol of hope for me and the gay community. We were not going to let this disease keep us in the closet. >> Yeah. >> But then there was also the fear that my dad would drive by and see me strutting my stuff down Santa Monica Boulevard. So I was always looking out for that brown truck with lawnmowers in the back. And when I was out there seeing on couches, my mom was not talking to me. And my dad, you know, who was notoriously homophobic, he's like, "You need to talk to him. You don't know what he's doing. He's going to die out there." And like, I mean, it's weird, right? The support just came out of nowhere because of what he said. I got invited for Christmas that year and I didn't know. I mean, my aunt told me it was your father who who spoke up and defended you. So, you know, I mean, I was just not made to be a gardener. I'm sorry. He just did not understand me, but he understood enough that I was who I was and I was not going to change. I just wanted to live. And I'm still alive. Thank God.

Sisters Shanita Baraka Akintonde and Danielle Tavon Bishop honor their mother, Mary Cathy Bishop, remembering her vibrant personality, unfiltered wisdom, and the small, meaningful moments that shaped their lives. From shared laughter in the kitchen to fulfilling her final wishes at home, they reflect on how her love, guidance, and spirit continue to inspire them every day.

Learn more: https://storycorps.org/stories/sisters-remember-mothers-legacy/
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en She was born in Brinkley, Arkansas, which I call Blinkley cuz if you blink, you'd miss it. She had dark ebony skin, bright brown eyes, and white white teeth. She painted her nails dark maroons and her lipstick matched that. And I remember when she kissed me, it left the lipstick on. >> It left that lipstick print. loved it. Mom didn't give two flying hoops whether you agreed with her. She was going to say what she wanted to say and if you got with it, great. If you didn't, peace. She would tell you the same story, >> but a different spin on it. >> It would be a different spin every time. And you did not interrupt her and say, "Mom, I've heard that story before." Right. >> Absolutely not. >> I literally studied everything from how she walked to how she talked because I thought she was amazing. The year before her passing, it was Thanksgiving and she took me in the kitchen. She told me specifically, "This is my last year cooking, so you need to learn how to do this." And I remember we stayed up to the early morning laughing, having a good time. And that was our last Thanksgiving. On her last days, she was in the hospital at this point, going in and out of consciousness. She said, "Take me home and make my room look like heaven." So, what we did was paint the walls a beautiful mauve color like a sunset. We made sure with the pillows that they were fluffed properly and that the sheets popped. When she came home, she looked around and smiled. I just wanted to savor that moment because I knew that meant she was happy with what we had done. She told us to get her two things. two drinks. >> Mhm. >> The cherry and the beer in a bottle. >> Not a can. >> And I said, "You can't have that. You're on medication." >> And remember she gave you >> She gave me a look and I said, "I'll be right back." >> I don't even know if she swallowed it. She just brought it up to her lips. And that night, she passed. The next year, that was my first Thanksgiving. and all of the family came over to my home and I tried to channel all that I could of my mom and now I feel like her hands come on top of me as I'm preparing a meals. You know, mom, she was my first real role model that I think I'm still evolving into being half the woman she was.

In 1993, three months into her pregnancy, Marla Wendel had a debilitating stroke. She went on to deliver a healthy son, Daniel, at 33 weeks. Twenty-five years later, Daniel and Marla sat down with StoryCorps to talk about those pivotal moments and how they shaped their relationship.

Learn more: https://storycorps.org/stories/a-mother-reflects-on-having-a-stroke-while-pregnant/
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en A lot of time went by between when you had your stroke and when I was born. What were you thinking during that time? >> I was just thinking, "We're going to make it. We're going to make it." At one point when I was pregnant, they were like, "Are you going to terminate the baby or not? It's risky to continue for your health, for the baby's health. And I was like, of course, we're going to keep the baby. >> And you have so much trouble making decisions about everything under the sun. >> I know >> you have trouble deciding what breakfast cereal. >> I know. I do. I do. That is true. But I felt so strongly you were supposed to be here. I was just thinking like, I want to be your mother. I want to be your mother so bad. >> Do you want to tell us about the stroke? >> It was a Saturday night. And as the night progressed, I noticed my leg was giving out. And you have an older sibling, so I started thinking like, I've got to get him into bed. And I feel bad, but I heaved him into the cage. >> You meant crib, right? >> Oh, what' I say? >> Cage. [laughter] >> I did. Yes. Thank you. >> You know, I was probably a teenager before I realized that not everyone has traumatic brain injuries. And that's not just some fun game me when she forgets words. But I always knew that you risked your life so that I could come into this world. That was always in the background. >> You had said that it made you feel pressured. >> Yeah. But pressured to do amazing things with your life. That's not a bad thing. >> Yes. But I never want amazing things like become the president of the United States or go to the moon. But like that you would bring joy to people because you have such a kind heart and you're such a good person. >> I mean, you had a pretty good example. >> That's good to hear. Thanks then. You're so strong inside. And if people see you, they might not know that because you're so quiet and thoughtful. If you weren't here with us, the world would not be as good of a place. Really truly, I can't think of it. It was a miracle that the two of us made it. >> [music]

Jeffrey Sherman and his wife, Wendy Liebman, remember his father, music composer Robert B. Sherman, and how getting a vaccine as a child sparked the creation of one of the most famous songs in the American canon.

Learn more: storycorps.org/stories/a-spoonful-of-sugar-how-a-vaccine-inspired-a-disney-classic
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en My dad always filtered everything down to its simplest form. People thought maybe he wasn't listening, but he would always listen. And then he would form his words very carefully. Words were like his religion. He brought word builders on my mom and dad's honeymoon. My mom complained. He wanted to just know words and he loved the sound of words and how they felt on your tongue. And my dad and uncle had a favorite song that they had created for Mary Poppins called The Eyes of Love. But Walt Disney said, "Could you write something that's more in line with the philosophy of Mary Poppins?" And it was all just falling flat. They were both really depressed. Well, it happened that that day I was at school. until I was about 6 years old and um they were giving us the oral polio vaccine uh you know wasn't the shot. So I you know stood in line with all my friends and we all just took this thing and then um I got home and my dad looked depressed and all the shades were closed. It was very dark in the house and I said, "Oh, we had the uh polio vaccine at school today." And he looked at me and he goes, "You let someone give you a shot at school? Did it hurt?" And I said, "No, no, no. They they took out this little cup and put a sugar cube in it and then dropped the medicine in it and you just ate it." And my dad looked at me and started shaking his head and he went over to the phone and he called Dick and told him he had something. And the next day they wrote, "A spoonful of sugar helps the medicine go down." They had this little recording studio my uncle usually would play and sometimes my dad would sing back up. Um, and so they would bring home the songs and I would hear all these songs before anybody else. And he played Spoonful of Sugar and he said, "Thank you for that song." I think that the love of his family and each of us kids inspired different things all the time for him. It was kind of like that was his yarn and he could make it into the most beautiful afghan. He could take the something mundane like that and see the the magic in it. [Music]

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Mary Lee McNelis was born with serious developmental delays. By age six, she still wasn't speaking. Dr. J. Herman Blake is descended from the Gullah people, known for their strong African roots, but didn’t grow up in one of their communities. In 1969, when he decided to spend Christmas on Daufuskie Island off the coast of South Carolina. There, the locals used a specific phrase to describe the holiday: “Making Christmas.” In a Brightness in Black conversation, he told his wife Dr. Emily Moore how his curiosity about what this meant got him in way over his head.

Learn more: https://storycorps.org/stories/holiday-escapade-gullah-town/
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en People said we make Christmas. And I didn't understand what that was. Christmas morning, a young lady came on her marsh tacky. What's that? >> Right. That's a horse. >> Oh. >> She knocked on the door and said, "You come over to Rehouse and y'all make Christmas." And I got to house and there's ham and there's chicken and there's greens, cornbread, there's beer and a little vodka as they call it. And then the man in that house said, "Let's we take a walk." And we went to somebody else's house and they said, "Welcome. Go to the table and make Christmas." And that day with this man, I went from house to house and the man of that house would welcome us. We'd eat and dine. And >> now would that man follow you? >> That man would join us. >> So then it would be three of you. >> By the time we got halfway through the day, it was about six or seven of us. In 1974, Darrell Anderson became the first male flight attendant for a small, up-and-coming airline. He faced discrimination for his gender and his race, but overcame it with kindness.

Learn more: https://storycorps.org/stories/flight-attendant-overcomes-madness/

And so I got hired. >> The pilots were really upset because it's always been pretty young steartesses that they could flirt with. And then they hired a male and he's black. >> I remember open up the cockpit and the pilots go, "Who in the hell are you?" [laughter] You know, there was a lot of different situations that happened on that airplane for me. And you get all types of people who fly. >> That's right. >> I had a guy on the flight going to Oklahoma City. So homeboy decided to call me Rabbit. You know, Rabbit, why don't you get me a drink? So I said, for me to hippity hop my butt up there, it's going to cost you. And he just thought that was funny. So he ended up buying everybody drinks. [laughter] I'd make him tip us every time I had to go get a drink. I turned his stupidity into paying us. Sisters Shanita Baraka Akintonde and Danielle Tavon Bishop honor their mother, Mary Cathy Bishop, remembering her vibrant personality, unfiltered wisdom, and the small, meaningful moments that shaped their lives. On the morning of January 29, 1998, nurse Emily Lyons went to her job at The New Woman All Women Health Care Clinic in Birmingham, Alabama. It was one of the few clinics providing abortions in the state. 

Shortly after she arrived, terrorist Eric Rufolph set off a homemade bomb filled with nails and gravel, severely injuring Emily and killing Robert "Sande" Sanderson, the police officer working security that day. Sande was the first person to be killed in an abortion clinic bombing in the U.S. Emily came to StoryCorps with her husband, Jeff, to remember that day.

StoryCorps is America's oral history project. And what better way to listen to America than from the road? In 2005, we converted an Airstream trailer into our traveling recording studio—our MobileBooth— and launched our first cross country tour. Each year, we visit places across the country to record the stories of people who live there. We partner with local public radio stations, cultural institutions, and community-based organizations to get the word out and invite people to bring someone to the MobileBooth. Our trained StoryCorps facilitators help set the scene for 40 minutes of uninterrupted, meaningful conversation between friends and loved ones. Life on the road means that we get to visit some extraordinary places and meet extraordinary people. And when the visit is done, we say goodbye, pack up the MobileBooth, get on the road, and head to our next destination.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en [Text] On August 29, 2005, Hurricane Katrina hit the Gulf Coast. Skip Boe witnessed the start of the storm from his home in Lakeview, New Orleans. Skip Boe: The wind started picking up, 50, 60 miles an hour. Then it gets past a hundred miles an hour, and then patio furniture's passing in front of your face, and people’s porches are going by. And then all of a sudden water just gushed in. I went upstairs to look out the window. Lo and behold, there's a fishing boat floating by. So I jumped out the window into the water and swam toward the boat. I tied it off, and I said, Imma deal with this in the morning. I took the comforter off of the bed, laid it on the roof. That was my bed for the night. I just thought I was the only idiot that stayed. And then I heard, “Can you help me?” And I shouted, “I'll get you tomorrow. Right now, can’t do anything at night time.” The next day, I proceeded to go get the Drakes who lived on the corner. They was probably in their eighties. She was totally out of it with Alzheimer's. They had made it to the attic. And then I heard my other neighbor calling me. And I kept yelling to him, “I'm coming to you next, Luke.” He just lived with his sister, who was bedridden, and when I pulled up, you could walk on his roof. The boat was gutter high. And I said, “Luke, it's Skip,” but he doesn't want to come out the attic. He says, “Don't you come down here, you killed my sister.” And I said, “No, I didn't, Luke.” He goes, “Well, she's downstairs. Why didn't you save me last night? Get outta here.” I think he lost it when he saw his sister get swallowed by water. Meanwhile, Mr. Drake's in the boat yelling, “I have to bring my wife to the hospital.” I said, “Luke, look, I'm coming back. Hang in there.” So, I left. And then I dropped them off to higher ground, that's when I said, I have to get back to get my buddy that I left. And uh, when I got back to Luke, he was dead in the attic. I cried. Second guessed myself. I made a decision, I picked the oldest ones first, thinking they were the weakest ones, leaving the strong to survive. And it didn’t work out that way. For months after, I was totally beating myself up. But later on, uh, I was cutting the grass, and the Drakes that were on the corner, their daughter passed by and said, “I think you saved my parents.” I said, “Yes ma’am, I did.” She goes, “You gave them three more years. I just wanted to tell you thank you.” And then I realized why I stayed during the storm, you know, what was the meaning of me staying. Rayford Junior Miles was a World War II veteran from Alabama who could come off as a classic tough guy. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Rayford Junior Miles — a World War II veteran from Alabama — could come off as a classic tough guy. But to his granddaughter Melanie Harrison (MH), he was just ‘Papa.’ At StoryCorps, Melanie sat down with her father, Jim Miles (JM), to remember her grandfather. MH: I remember, I was young enough to be in a high chair. Papa got me out and gave me his chewing tobacco kiss. There were a lot of them, but they were appreciated. JM: His grandmothers taught him to chew when he was like eight years old or something. And my father was an expert at flipping you off. Now he didn't do it out of meanness— just kidding around, he'd shoot you a bird. And if he was really, really on a thing there, he'd shoot two at the same time— bang, bang! And they were crisp, they snapped. It was a work of art. So a couple days before he died, when I was up visiting the hospital, we talked for 15 minutes and I said, ‘Well, we got, we gotta go now.’ And he didn't nod or anything. He just bang, bang, just flipped those birds out. And as we were coming home, I looked into the sky and I saw a cosmic finger. It was a gigantic dark cloud formation, it was a perfect bird. And I said, Mel, look at this. And then you looked at it and you said, ‘Oh my God.’ And you told me today that you think that was just my father's last bird. I'm outta here. MH: I'm done. That was fun. JM: Honest, it was there. It was the clearest cloud formation I've ever seen. MH: Whenever I, I see a big cloudy day, and big storm clouds roll past... I look for 'em . You know, right after he died, I had a dream that I was in the house. And he was just sitting there with his hands across his belly, like he usually did. Just looking at me. Like, y’know, ‘It's cool.’ JM: ‘You'll be okay.’ MH: Yeah. JM: Hm. That’s something to think about. MH: My name is Melanie Harrison. It's been 14 years since I had that conversation with my dad. He passed away in 2019. My dad looked like Santa Claus, and at six foot six, he was a gentle giant. I loved going places with him and letting everybody see like, "oh, that's why she's so tall!" I think when my dad saw the finger in the sky, it helped him process what was upcoming. He may not have shared it was something he was struggling with, but we knew. He knew he would have to step up and help take care of his mom. And all of the changes that come along when a parent dies. And the cloud was like my Papa saying… ‘You’re gonna be all right.’ When my dad passed, I had dreams very similar to the dream that I had of his father, after he passed— he just kind of smiled, and let me know that it was okay. As the years go by, I don't have as many dreams, but both of them pop up in there every now and then. They're little things that help you remember that you're gonna be able to move forward. And it's… it’s always good to see them again. [Text] Follow us. Twitter. Facebook. Instagram. And watch more on YouTube. [Logo] StoryCorps. [Logo] Corporation for Public Broadcasting. On The TODAY Show, Tony Goldwyn, Octavia Spencer and Jenna Bush Hager shared something that feels rare on national television: hope. They sat down to discuss Tony’s experiences with One Small Step, a project from StoryCorps that brings people with different political beliefs together for one respectful, face-to-face conversation.

They believe, like we do, that real conversations, even with people we disagree with, can change hearts, build bridges, and remind us of our shared humanity.

It can be so powerful to show up and care when it feels easier to walk away, and to see what happens when we swap assumptions for real conversation.

We don’t have to agree on everything to start seeing each other more clearly. And it doesn’t take a sweeping act, just one step.

What happens when a progressive LGBTQ+ news creator and a Christian leadership coach sit down to talk, not debate?

On the morning of January 29, 1998, nurse Emily Lyons went to her job at The New Woman All Women Health Care Clinic in Birmingham, Alabama. It was one of the few clinics providing abortions in the state. 

Shortly after she arrived, terrorist Eric Rufolph set off a homemade bomb filled with nails and gravel, severely injuring Emily and killing Robert "Sande" Sanderson, the police officer working security that day. Sande was the first person to be killed in an abortion clinic bombing in the U.S. Emily came to StoryCorps with her husband, Jeff, to remember that day.

Since 2005, our iconic Airstream-turned-recording studio has crisscrossed the country, capturing stories from towns large and small—ensuring every voice is heard.

Join us on our journey to recording America’s stories: storycorps.org/mobile-tour
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en People come to StoryCorps to record an interview with someone they love, and those recordings are archived at the American Folk Life Center at the Library of Congress, so that future generations can hear the stories and the voices of today. StoryCorps is America's oral history project. And what better way to listen to America than from the road? In 2005, we converted an Airstream trailer into our traveling recording studio—our MobileBooth— and launched our first cross country tour. Each year, we visit places across the country to record the stories of people who live there. We partner with local public radio stations, cultural institutions, and community-based organizations to get the word out and invite people to bring someone to the MobileBooth. Our trained StoryCorps facilitators help set the scene for 40 minutes of uninterrupted, meaningful conversation between friends and loved ones. Life on the road means that we get to visit some extraordinary places and meet extraordinary people. And when the visit is done, we say goodbye, pack up the MobileBooth, get on the road, and head to our next destination.

And I was like, trying so hard to learn, uh, you know, how to be right in, in this idea and how to fix it in this idea. I remember it went on for several weeks, um, and I ended up going to confession and Father Kelly was the head of the church that that I went to and... I was just crying because I was like, "Father Kelly, I'm trying so hard and it's not working and it's not that I'm not trying and I'm afraid you're gonna think I'm not trying." He's like, "No, I know you're trying, you're a good kid." Like, "Okay, relax kid," like, 'cause I was always so nervous about everything. Um, and I was like, "I just think that maybe I should, uh... If I can't get it in the next couple of weeks, I think maybe my parents would rather just remember me as the child they knew, instead of have to experience me as the adult I think I'm gonna end up." And he was like — opened the little thing and he was like, "Don't... you... dare. Don't you dare think that you, one, need to be fixed. This is an option. This is something that the church does. You are loved. You are a good kid. You're a very nervous kid, but we can't think like that, right? So now what you're telling me is you're thinking about maybe you don't wanna be alive anymore." And I was like, "Yeah." And he was like, "I would ra" — he's like, "I accept you. How about that, right now? I'll accept you right now and I'll talk to your mom about it." And I was like, "Okay." And that man, like, really saved my life. So I had actually a quite good experience with the church and coming out; better than I had with a lot of other people. But throughout the rest of my year, af — life after that experience, it got harder with people who didn't maybe have a Father Kelly in their life to teach 'em that somebody was, you know, worth living and worth loving, even if they weren't what your idea of "right" was. BRENDA HARKINS: Wow... well, I love Father Kelly and I'm thankful for him. Um, yeah, I think that it's really, um, made me sad when I heard you say that you just wanted to get fixed. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Because I think that we too often look at each other, look at people, whatever the situation is, and we think they're a problem to solve instead of a person to love. And really, it's only like we, we are... every single one of us transformed, transformed so much more by who we love than anything else. And so I love it that Father Kelly loved you. And, uh... V SPEHAR: Well, I wanna, so to put it back to you, you know, you have seven children, blended family, lots of bonus kids — what, what makes people gravitate towards you, which some folks might think is an anomaly, you know, because a lot of folks are afraid of, you know, people who are forward with their religion. How have you navigated... having all these people come to you and trust you? BRENDA HARKINS: I think that there's a sense that, um, I like to provide a safe environment for people, and I'd love for people to know they're loved. And one of the things I do even in business is, um, help teams figure out the differences within the team that helps them to be, uh, better who they are together. And so I think that's just what I've done in life, all of my life. I look at the awesomeness about people and I draw it out. I love to mine the gold in people. That's what I really love to do, because I believe every single one of us has treasure inside of us. And so I think when, when people do that with you, you know, like if somebody comes up to you and they're, they, they genuinely love you, you feel the authenticity and you feel the safeness and they're calling out what's great about you. I mean, who doesn't wanna be in a relationship with that? I do. You know? V SPEHAR: Do you think it's difficult to. Interact with other folks, you know, in Texas, right? Which has some really strict right-wing laws, um, or within the church or within your community who maybe aren't as welcoming as you. Like, how do you navigate that space? BRENDA HARKINS: Well, I've got people who don't like me on all sides. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: And I've got people who do on all sides. So, you know, it's a win-win. Um, there are, um, people who have strong convictions that political issues are spiritual issues, and I disagree with that. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: And so that has not made me some friends within the church world. Um... and then I've had some challenges with others who, um... I have friends, I have family who are in relationships that are gay, relationships that are married, that are, and I love them dearly. And we're friends and we — and we're family too, by the way. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Um, and so... You know, a lot of times they wish that I would stand up and speak out for who they are and what, and I'm like, "Well, those are your convictions and that's for you to stand up and speak out for. I'll stand up for you 'cause I love you, but you know: you are the one that stands up for your convictions, and I'll stand up for mine, and we'll stand up for each other in relationship and love each other really well through all the differences. So I don't know if that answered your question or not. V SPEHAR: Yeah, it surely does. I think a lot though about the crossover between major political movements and the idea of religious broadly. Right? So like when we think about the women's suffrage movement, a lot of that came out of, um, the Quakers of, uh, Western New York. Or when we think about the civil rights movement, Dr. King was a Baptist preacher. I do think there is like a big crossover between politics and religion when it comes to advancing humanity that a lot of folks, um... I think rightly right now, feel stuck up against, because there's not like the establishment that's so clear. And then the counter movement, maybe the way there was in like the sixties and seventies, and now it's kind of like, um, you know, you might look at some of the stuff that, let's say... Donald Trump does and say, um, "Well, is that in line with a counter movement that perpetuates humanity? Is that in line with Christian values or can we pick and choose? Can we separate the art from the artist?" And for me, sometimes it's, no, we can't separate, um, you know, some of the convictions that somebody has when it comes to politics from the way they claim to be religiously. BRENDA HARKINS: No, I totally agree. I, I agree with that. I agree a hundred percent with that. V SPEHAR: What do you think influenced your, like, personal political beliefs the most? Like did you have a moment as an adult where you were like, "Hey, I think this is where I'm going, this is where I feel I most fit in"? BRENDA HARKINS: Well, first of all, I'm not a terribly political person. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: I'm more of a... I love, uh, faith, family, friends, west Texas sunsets, and great coffee. I mean, I love that, you know, and, um, and the other issues, I do... I vote of course, right? But I'm just not a political activist. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: And I'd love to hear more about you on that subject, but I think that for my personal beliefs, what influenced me the most is probably my dad, who actually, for a lot of my — from 12 to 18, we didn't even speak. V SPEHAR: Mmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Um, but the years before and the years that were restored after, um, helped me see who he was and, um... he was, he was someone who grew up extreme — in extreme poverty, who was given a pair of shoes by a dentist and decided when he grew up he was gonna be a dentist. And he did. And you know, he just, uh, he put his mind to things and he did them, and he loved people so big, uh, in all walks of life. And I think that that probably personally has been what has influenced me the most. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah, please tell me about you. I would love to know — personally or politically or both, right? I would love to know about you. V SPEHAR: So for me, unfortunately, like my mere existence is political now, right? Everybody has an idea about gay people, what rights they should or shouldn't have, what type of inherent rights their marriages should or shouldn't have. So every single day I don't get the sort of like option to opt out of, of being political because my very existence has been made political. Um, I got my early ideas about politics from my dad who was a military contractor, and we come from a deeply patriotic military-type family, and I... you know, was little during the Desert Storm wars, and it was my first week in college in New York City when 9/11 happened. And so I have had this like very front-row seat to what patriotism from the 90s and early 2000s was, versus what it's become now. Um, and I still believe myself to be a deeply patriotic person. I mean, like, this is my office, right? Like it's very... BRENDA HARKINS: I love it. I love it so much. V SPEHAR: It's very that way, you know? Um, and I think I tend to look at political figures as deeply human figures and not these like, you know, uh, folks up on a pedestal who were omnipotent and they knew everything. I'm like... I don't think so. I think they were human people making human decisions a lot of the time. And that brings me a lot of peace. I started off as a Republican, which I had to explain to Obama one time to his face when we were making a TikTok together. And he was like, "Well, you voted for me, right?" And I was like, "Uh, no sir. I — I was like 19 and my dad took me and we voted for, of course, John McCain, 'cause that was, like, my dad's hero-type person." And then the next time I was working for Mitt Romney as a caterer for the 2012 RNC. And I just really thought he was great because when he was governor of Massachusetts, he was the first governor to sign in gay marriage. And that was like, I was a single-issue voter. I wanted to vote at, I think it was like 20... well, what was it, like 25 at that time or something? That I really wanted gay marriage to be legal. And um, so we, so we did that. And uh, I voted for Romney. And I remember being backstage one time, and this is when I sort of switched from Republican to Democrat. Um, and Romney was asking the catering staff like, "Are you gonna vote for me?" And I was like, "Yes." And I told him because of the gay marriage thing. And he was like, "Yeah, that was — I don't know why people are so bothered, why they wanna be involved in other people's bedrooms. That's just not something I wanna spend my eight years dealing with, so I'm — I don't wanna deal with it." I thought that was great. And then he went on stage and he said the exact opposite, right? 'Cause he had to kind of appease the Tea Party and I was devastated because I'd really believed him. Um, and then, you know, you start to learn from politics how they all play the game behind the scenes. And then I changed to be a Democrat when in 20... um... 15, that we got gay marriage through the Obergefell decision. And I just felt more aligned with that party because they had shown me the action that I had so desperately wanted. Um... I think that there are issues in the Democratic Party just the same as there were in the Republican Party, and I think that they benefit greatly, both sides, from... That's why I wanted to do this, Brenda, because they benefit so greatly from being like, "Brenda and V will never talk. Nope. They would tear each other's hair out. There could never ever be a time in which these people could find common ground. And we already have like five times now, right? So... BRENDA HARKINS: Right. V SPEHAR: That's what I think is interesting about politics. Um, and I think the "all or nothing of it" has become so pervasive to folks that there's gonna be people who watch my show who are gonna be like, "I can't believe you went on there and risked potentially talking to somebody who we don't agree with." And I'm like, "I know. Uh. I also had Marianne Williamson on this morning, so you know, we go, we go all over the place over here." BRENDA HARKINS: Well, I think if we don't talk to people who don't agree with us, that we never grow, if all we do is surround ourself with people who have the same position, also there's no influence. You just have a bunch of cheerleaders around you with, you know, like what influence is there if people already agree with you? Like, let's build some bridges and, and get a bigger perspective on all of this. By the way, you did say that you came from a patriotic family. Mm-hmm. And I wanna ask you what that means to you. Like what is patriotism to you? V SPEHAR: It's a lot of things. So in particular, it's like... my dad's a really good singer and he used to, like, anytime we would have a problem, he'd take us for rides in the Jeep, which would inevitably end with him singing "Proud to be an American" or something from Lee Greenwood at the end. And 'cause he was, but he had this idea that men in particular are only allowed a certain avenues to release their emotions. And that was like, when you love a woman or love your country, those are the only two times that you can be in any way sort of like... exuberant about the way you feel. And so, um, I learned a lot from him about patriotism. Um, and I also learned the difference between like patriotism and national pride and how those things can be different. You can believe in your country and want the best for it, and also, uh, be able to point out when somebody's not doing the right thing for it, and not just be so beholden to a personality or a politician that you don't put country first. And I think putting country first oftentimes means putting people first. And this is where I could get a little bit, uh, you know, into it with the Republican side who, um, sometimes thinks things like Medicaid or SNAP benefits or the way that we provide aid to other countries isn't putting America first. But to me, I always liked being the hero. Like my whole lens has been from the idea that, like going back to my grandparents, right? Um, when people who were in these concentration camps heard American voices, they knew that they were saved, right? That was the end. When you hear American voices, you should feel safe. And so that's my perspective on politics and patriotism, and that's what I hope to continue to perpetuate. And I worry nowadays that sometimes when they hear American voices here or abroad that they don't feel safe anymore. BRENDA HARKINS: Mmm. That's good. V SPEHAR: What about you? BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah, well, patriotism, a lot of that goes back to my dad as well. He was... V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: You know, he was extremely patriotic. I remember the songs, I remember all of that. I remember tears in his eyes, which I never saw that I would see... V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: ...was singing those songs. And, um, and I guess to me it means, um. Loving your coun — country, but not to the... well, I don't think love is ever being blind to the faults of it. So loving your country and in, in the way that you see, um, you can help make it better to do that. I, I actually think this that we're doing is one of those ways. V SPEHAR: So from this conversation, I know I'm gonna like, you know, call my wife and my friends and be like, "I met the most lovely lady from Texas today." How will having a conversation with me sort of like change the way you feel maybe about the way that religion and politics intersect, or about the way we reach out to people? BRENDA HARKINS: I think more than change it, it will affirm the importance of it, V. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: I feel like, um, I feel like I'd love to sit down and have a cup of coffee with you when we're not being recorded, and I just... V SPEHAR: I know. Well, you can, they'll give you my phone number. They have it. BRENDA HARKINS: Okay. V SPEHAR: I talk to people all day. That's my job. BRENDA HARKINS: No, I, I would love, um, yeah, I would love to get to know you better. And I feel like that is one of the things that... I mean, you have affirmed that to me today, because I didn't know. I never know when I get on one of these conversations how it's gonna go and... it's another person that's a beautiful human that has a lot of gold inside of 'em, and I've seen that today, and I appreciate that, and I thank you for like... sharing so much of who you are with me today. So, I don't know, does that answer your question? V SPEHAR: Yes, absolutely. Um, my other, my other question is, you know, we talked about first impressions when we read each other's bio, but when my background came up, right, and knowing just what you knew about me, was any of this a surprise to you that this is like the kind of stuff that I would — someone with my bio surrounds themself with? BRENDA HARKINS: Oh no, but you know what, it wasn't a surprise to me. I loved it that I saw Lincoln back there. I love your smiley cup and that eagle — I will have to take a picture and send you my, the, the door knocker on my... V SPEHAR: Oh, right on. BRENDA HARKINS: ...looks almost exactly like that. V SPEHAR: Yeah. BRENDA HARKINS: And it was on my husband's great-great-grandfather's house or something like that, so. V SPEHAR: Wow. BRENDA HARKINS: Um, I'm like, "Wow! Already we have an eagle in common, you know?" V SPEHAR: I know! BRENDA HARKINS: Um, so no, it didn't surprise me 'cause I didn't really have any... I don't, I ne — I don't ever really have any preconceived ideas. My main concern is that we connect. V SPEHAR: Right, right. BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah. V SPEHAR: So of all the kids that you have, do they share your political and religious beliefs too? BRENDA HARKINS: Oh goodness, no! Goodness no. V SPEHAR: No, they don't? How do you handle that? BRENDA HARKINS: No, not all of them, my goodness. Um, so we've got — so I had three, my husband had two when we got married. We've had two together. We have 12 grandchildren. I have one great-grandbaby. I cannot believe that. That's ridiculous... V SPEHAR: Wow! BRENDA HARKINS: ...And wonderful. Ridiculous, and wonderful. Um. So, yeah, we've got all different perspectives, like from... way far left to way far right. And Thanksgiving is fun. Now, we, we do love each other and we, um — for a lot of our gatherings, we just choose to leave those differences out and love each other and have fun together. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Um, and then some of them like to... blow up things by dropping a bomb and seeing what'll happen, you know? So, um... V SPEHAR: How do you navigate that? Like when there is a disagreement with people, you know, at the holiday? BRENDA HARKINS: I listen and I ask questions. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah. I, I listen for what... I li — I usually try to listen for why they did it, um, why they started it. And then I ask what's important to them about that. And then I really listen 'cause I really care. V SPEHAR: Mmm. BRENDA HARKINS: I really do. I mean, I may not agree, but they may s — sway me, you know? Like... I'm not so grounded in where I'm at that I, I don't look at other perspectives and, and incorporate that into who I am. So... V SPEHAR: Is there any like example you could give of, sometime you think somebody, like, dropped a bomb and how you guys got through it? BRENDA HARKINS: Oh, I hate those spur-of-the-moment questions and I've gotta think of... V SPEHAR: I know. BRENDA HARKINS: Um... let me be thinking about it while I ask you, okay? V SPEHAR: Sure! BRENDA HARKINS: I'll be, be trying to think about that. But — how do you navigate disagreements? Like, do you have that within your family? It sounds like you might from the background, and how do you navigate that? V SPEHAR: So my family — um, I, I feel like... used to fight more when I was younger. My mom had the energy for it. Now we don't. Um, there's a lot of like, "We just don't see those people anymore. We just don't choose to have those fights anymore." And on the other side, on my wife's family, we've been "no contact" with her parents for quite some time. And that came after years and years and years and years of begging them to... show up with kindness or tolerance at a minimum, and their continued commitment to make themself the victim of like, having to endure being at an event with my gay marriage to their daughter, that they didn't necessarily fully understand, that they constantly wanted to question, that they constantly wanted to question her... Um, and it just got to a point where it... Honestly, it's like one of the greatest heartbreaks, the most difficult thing I think a lot of people think going "no contact" will be easier. And it's not. BRENDA HARKINS: No. V SPEHAR: It is the greatest, perpetual, constant reoccurring grief that a family can go through and to have it go on for so long without the other side breaking is just... Brenda, like... the hardest thing because like, we don't have children, but we want them soon. And I can't imagine if my child said to me, "You've hurt me so gravely that I need to take space from you," that I wouldn't give them the space and then like, I don't know, camp out on their lawn to be like, "I'm so sorry. I'll do anything to like — to like — please, I, it's me. I, I will take all the blame, like I just can't live like this." But to, to be sort of like continually rejected, um, is very difficult. So that's how... BRENDA HARKINS: Yes. V SPEHAR: ...our holidays sometimes go. A lot of tears. A lot of tears in a "no-contact" family. When you think that you'll get relief, each time you think, "Well, this time it won't be as bad," and every time it's really hard. BRENDA HARKINS: Wow. I'm so sorry for that. V SPEHAR: Mmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah. The, the separation, the closing people out: that's "the loud," that is "the loud," the, there is so much loudness in that silence right there, in that separation. There's so much that's just screaming. Um, it... hmm. V SPEHAR: And it comes down to people's allegiance, right? Like, will you, will, in this case, will you decide that your allegiance is to the president — um, whether he's actively the president at that moment or not — or to your child? And I think it's really difficult for some people, and I, I do wonder how they get to that point, and why it's so hard seemingly to come back from it to say that, like, their allegiance to a president, um, and that person's very far right ideals, supersedes their ability to love their child anymore. That's something that I, I have like a really difficult time understanding or finding space for, which is how you end up "no contact," because it's like, "How many more ways can I ask you to love me?" Right? Or in this case, my wife asked her parents to love her and to keep — be continually rejected until she comes around, and it's like, "Comes around to what? The man wants to get rid of gay marriage by June. How am I gonna come around to that? It seems like maybe you guys gotta come around a little bit this way and maybe we're — find a closer middle." But for a lot of families that just hasn't happened. BRENDA HARKINS: Well, and that's where when you have issues that become more important than loving relationships, it's, uh... it's heartbreaking, it's devastating, and... V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. Is that something — you'd never let that happen with your kids? BRENDA HARKINS: No. V SPEHAR: Yeah. BRENDA HARKINS: No. V SPEHAR: Are we getting an invite to Christmas, Brenda? I feel like... BRENDA HARKINS: Come to Texas for Christmas! Oh my gosh, that would be so fun. V SPEHAR: You just picked up two more, right? BRENDA HARKINS: Maybe we'll do that. V SPEHAR: It has been such a treat to chat. BRENDA HARKINS: I mean, you're welcome! I will say that! V SPEHAR: So what has surprised you from this chat now that we're at the end of our chat? BRENDA HARKINS: Um, that — well that I haven't asked more questions. You've been talking and asking me and I haven't asked you nearly enough and I wanna hear more. Um... What has surprised me? I think what has delighted me is a better word, is that, um, that you seem like a delightful person. That you seem like a very caring person and, um... and that, that makes me very happy. I am, I, I, I am delighted that I feel that there was a connection here, and I hope it will continue. V SPEHAR: Absolutely. BRENDA HARKINS: What about you? What have you — what surprised you? V SPEHAR: I gotta tell you, it might be, it might be like another arrow in the quiver today to be like, I'm — this nice lady Brenda, who has, you know, fairly conservative and Jesus-forward values also understands that you don't abandon your children for a president. So I feel like I've got one more example of not being crazy, and that is a huge gift to me because sometimes you can feel so alone, with not knowing that many people who you think are on the opposite side of the aisle of you — be that for religion or politics or just like lifestyle or anything, um — but there are these universal truths that we need to continue to remind each other of, which are like, no, you love your family more than anything, and your children more than anything. And politics comes and goes, and what we wanna do is make sure that we're presenting, like, the best, safest America. We all — both agreed on that. Um... BRENDA HARKINS: Yes we did. V SPEHAR: And so I feel, I feel really, um... sort of like, lightened by that — that, you know, the times in which we see so much hate online, or we see so much resistance and grief in our real lives are maybe — maybe there's not as much more of that out there. Uh, and maybe there's a lot more good out there and we should be trying to build that together as a society, as opposed to trying to assume that everybody is, um, you know, as hateful as the most hateful person we've ever met. BRENDA HARKINS: Yes! I think that there — I think we honestly do have so much more. People in general have so much more in common than they have different, and we just need to take the time to talk about these things instead of keeping that "us and them" mentality. Um, let's get to know each other before we make those assumptions, so. V SPEHAR: Well, that's it for me and Brenda, who are starting a new podcast next week where we help you with your family! Thank you very much, Brenda; it's been a pleasure to get to chat with you, um, and your family's very lucky to have you. You just seem like such a, a bright light, um, keeping everybody together, and that's just, that's what we need out here. More of that. BRENDA HARKINS: Oh, it's been a joy to meet you, and I look forward to connecting with you again! V SPEHAR: Yeah, absolutely. BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah. Yeah. Okay. Well, all the best to you. V SPEHAR: You too. BRENDA HARKINS: Bye-bye. See you Christmas. V SPEHAR: Yes. See you at Christmas and uh, you know, I might give you my mother-in-law's phone number... Give her a little call. Be like, "Hey, woman-to-woman, in the peer group. Knock it off." BRENDA HARKINS: Okay, we'll see you. Bye-bye.

August 29, 2025 marks 20 years since Hurricane Katrina hit the Gulf Coast. In Lakeview, New Orleans, Skip Boe watched the storm unfold from his home. He told StoryCorps about the neighbors he rescued from the wreckage, and his regret around one he couldn’t save.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en [Text] On August 29, 2005, Hurricane Katrina hit the Gulf Coast. Skip Boe witnessed the start of the storm from his home in Lakeview, New Orleans. Skip Boe: The wind started picking up, 50, 60 miles an hour. Then it gets past a hundred miles an hour, and then patio furniture's passing in front of your face, and people’s porches are going by. And then all of a sudden water just gushed in. I went upstairs to look out the window. Lo and behold, there's a fishing boat floating by. So I jumped out the window into the water and swam toward the boat. I tied it off, and I said, Imma deal with this in the morning. I took the comforter off of the bed, laid it on the roof. That was my bed for the night. I just thought I was the only idiot that stayed. And then I heard, “Can you help me?” And I shouted, “I'll get you tomorrow. Right now, can’t do anything at night time.” The next day, I proceeded to go get the Drakes who lived on the corner. They was probably in their eighties. She was totally out of it with Alzheimer's. They had made it to the attic. And then I heard my other neighbor calling me. And I kept yelling to him, “I'm coming to you next, Luke.” He just lived with his sister, who was bedridden, and when I pulled up, you could walk on his roof. The boat was gutter high. And I said, “Luke, it's Skip,” but he doesn't want to come out the attic. He says, “Don't you come down here, you killed my sister.” And I said, “No, I didn't, Luke.” He goes, “Well, she's downstairs. Why didn't you save me last night? Get outta here.” I think he lost it when he saw his sister get swallowed by water. Meanwhile, Mr. Drake's in the boat yelling, “I have to bring my wife to the hospital.” I said, “Luke, look, I'm coming back. Hang in there.” So, I left. And then I dropped them off to higher ground, that's when I said, I have to get back to get my buddy that I left. And uh, when I got back to Luke, he was dead in the attic. I cried. Second guessed myself. I made a decision, I picked the oldest ones first, thinking they were the weakest ones, leaving the strong to survive. And it didn’t work out that way. For months after, I was totally beating myself up. But later on, uh, I was cutting the grass, and the Drakes that were on the corner, their daughter passed by and said, “I think you saved my parents.” I said, “Yes ma’am, I did.” She goes, “You gave them three more years. I just wanted to tell you thank you.” And then I realized why I stayed during the storm, you know, what was the meaning of me staying. And, at least I know that I did the best that a person could have done. [Text] Follow us. Twitter. Facebook. Instagram. And watch more on YouTube. description:

What happens when you sit down with someone you’ve been told you’ll never understand?
Liberal actor and activist Tony Goldwyn and conservative nonprofit leader and father Ben Sauceda couldn’t come from more different political worlds.

But, in their One Small Step conversation, they demonstrate something many of us are craving right now: how to stay open, stay curious, and make space for shared humanity, even when you disagree. 

In a time when it feels easier to retreat into our corners, this conversation shows us what’s possible when we step outside of them.

Know someone who believes in bridging divides through conversation? This is the one to send their way.

Then ask yourself: who might surprise you if you gave them a chance to speak?

Follow @takeonesmallstep to stay inspired and hopeful.
#OneSmallStep #TonyGoldwyn #ConversationsThatMatter #HumanFirst #ListenToUnderstand #StoryCorps

Listen to more of their conversation: https://youtube.com/shorts/rKPlAdsULk8
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US BEN SAUCEDA: Hello! How are you? TONY GOLDWYN: I'm Tony! How you doin'? BEN SAUCEDA: Ben, nice to meet you. TONY GOLDWYN: Nice to meet you, Ben. BEN SAUCEDA: Thank you. JONATHAN Z: Welcome! TONY GOLDWYN: A treat... BEN SAUCEDA: Yes, thank you. TONY GOLDWYN: ...to get to do this, yeah. BEN SAUCEDA: I'm excited about this. TONY GOLDWYN: Me too. I hope to have an interesting conversation to make contact with someone I don't know. I don't really have any fears, uh... except that I don't have any idea where this conversation's headed, but that's always exciting. BEN SAUCEDA: My name is Ben Sauceda, I am 41, and I'm here in New York City with Tony Goldwyn, who is my One Small Step partner today. TONY GOLDWYN: Ben, um, was born and raised in Wichita, Kansas, firstborn to a first-generation American Hispanic family, and is the CEO of a prominent nonprofit in Wichita. BEN SAUCEDA: And this is Tony's bio: he's been married to his wife Jane for almost 38 years — that's incredible — and has two daughters, Anna and Tess. Tony grew up in Los Angeles, uh, but has lived in the tri-state since college. Uh, Tony is an actor and director in the entertainment industry. TONY GOLDWYN: Okay, so first question is: Ben, why did you sign up for One Small Step? BEN SAUCEDA: So, for me it was really important to have dialogue and conversations with people who, who have different opinions and beliefs than I do. TONY GOLDWYN: It is so important for me to, to... have con — be in conversation with people, particularly people who might look at the world in a different way than I do, to challenge myself to listen and see another perspective. And, um, I'm very concerned in our country today and in our society in general, for many, many reasons, we've stopped listening to each other, and stopped learning how to talk to each other, and people are afraid to talk to each other. BEN SAUCEDA: There are extremes on both sides, no doubt, that don't have the same end goal. But I would say you could probably say that 80% of Americans have the same end goal. Just the avenues in which we're getting there looks different. So how do or did your politics and general beliefs, um, differ from your parents or your family? TONY GOLDWYN: My father was actually a Republican for much of my life. BEN SAUCEDA: Okay. TONY GOLDWYN: But my mom and my stepfather were very — you know, ardent and sometimes strident Democrats. Uh, and I grew up through Watergate and all that as a seminal kind of experience. It was about, you know, uh, when I started to be awakening to politics and when I was a small kid, the Vietnam War. And, and, and so there was a, it was a very, um, politically tumultuous time when I was a young kid. So we had a lot of very spirited, um, conversations around the dinner tables in, in my family. BEN SAUCEDA: Interestingly enough, my parents were not political. So I will say as a second-generation Hispanic involved in the Hispanic community back home, yes, it is assumed that I should be a liberal Democrat. My mom leans conservative. Uh, my dad is kind of indifferent and I — my dad didn't register to vote till 2012 or 2010. Um, and he's only voted I think three times. Uh, twice was when I ran for office, and so he had to vote for me. Like, "That was kind of the deal, Dad!" TONY GOLDWYN: Ben, is there something that gives you hope for the future? I'm guessing talking to you that there's a lot that gives you hope for the future! BEN SAUCEDA: There is a lot. So again, for me, faith is such a central part of my life. I, I've grown up that way, but I — it's, it's become personal and real for me. And so to that degree, my faith is truly what gives me hope. What about for you? What, what... TONY GOLDWYN: I, I feel exactly the same way. Faith is a big one and it's, um — uh, I'm not formally religious, I was not raised in a religious tradition, but I have tremendous faith in humanity. BEN SAUCEDA: Yeah. TONY GOLDWYN: And, uh, that, that is a deeply spiritual dimension for me. I know that when people put down, put aside their assumptions about other people and just talk, the miracles happen. I, I feel that we all need to, um, take responsibility for that. And so I have a, I have a lot of faith that, um, most people, uh, crave that. BEN SAUCEDA: Yeah. Yeah, I agree. I think the more that we talk and the more that you just have these conversations, people realize that we have a lot more in common than what divides us. TONY GOLDWYN: Yeah. Look, it's why I do what I do for a living. I mean, I'm a storyteller for a living, and I've seen the impact of when you tell stories, that completely transcends politics and presumption. You see, you get inside other people's lives and experience their experience in a subjective way, and it changes you. BEN SAUCEDA: Yeah. TONY GOLDWYN: Um. And um, and people who relate to the — who, maybe you're telling a story that's related to their life, they feel seen. That's what we all want: to see and be seen. BEN SAUCEDA: Exactly. Exactly. I appreciate this. This has been fantastic. TONY GOLDWYN: Yeah, likewise. Likewise. BEN SAUCEDA: Yeah. I think one of the things I learned today about Tony was just: I've always had preconceived notions going to that there about someone in the film industry. Tony's just a great down-to-earth individual that you could have a great conversation with, really. Uh, it was something I took away from today. TONY GOLDWYN: My conversation with Ben really, um, confirmed for me my belief and, and strong instinct that people are so multifaceted and complex that the things that di — where we differ is a beautiful thing. It's... like that's, that's a positive, um, to interact with people who, who are — have different beliefs from different cultures, a different worldview, uh, um... And you'll inevitably find that there are endless similarities as well.

In 2020, Ingrid Hoch and Brian Lahr were hired as managers on a construction project at the San Diego International Airport. But before the job officially began, COVID hit. In the midst of the pandemic, Ingrid and Brian had to find ways to foster community and keep up morale. At StoryCorps, they remembered how the tiny insects that spread their wings helped them do just that. As heard on NPR's "Morning Edition" on Friday, July 11th, 2025.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] In 2020, Ingrid Hoch (IH) and Brian Lahr (BL) were hired as managers on a big construction project: creating a brand new terminal at the San Diego International Airport. But before the job had officially begun, COVID hit. Ingrid and Brian had to find ways to keep morale up in the middle of the pandemic. At StoryCorps, they remembered how some tiny insects helped them do just that. IH: When I came back to work in person, it was still masks, it was still distance. And so we planted a vegetable garden that would bring us together. And in early summer, we started to notice that there were four caterpillars. BL: And they kept getting bigger and bigger, and once word got out, people were like, ‘Hey, hey check out the caterpillars.’ I mean, you got guys who are walking around with hard hats, looking at these little four caterpillars every day. IH: Workers go out there and they're just like, ‘You know what? I just feel more at peace when I'm watching these things.’ Soon enough all the little guys make their chrysalis. And it's a beautiful lime green cocoon, but then within 24 hours, they turn translucent. BL: And your first thought is ‘Oh, crap, it died.’ But, you stare at it and then they start coming out. It's crazy. So then I said, ‘Why don't we just make the whole thing into a monarch butterfly enclosure type thing?’ We got some of the toughest guys you've ever seen working out there in the field, the next thing you know, they're saying, ‘When are you gonna release the butterflies?’ The day we did their big release party, probably over a hundred people come to watch us. IH: We thought there'd be a flurry of butterflies that just explode but they do not do that, they're like, more cautious. People came down, we're like, ‘If you wanna like let one get on your finger,’ and then, it's the most delicate touch of those little legs. And there was such joy and so many smiles. That next year we had 120 monarchs. And then last year we had 350 monarchs. And this year we're hoping for 600 plus. BL: So what is it you wanna take away from the job when you leave? IH: That I cared about the people. I know the job, that's why we're here. But I think getting something done is not the point of living. And, we will all be transformed, those who worked on this project. We can look at that transformation that butterflies go through: from an egg to caterpillar to that chrysalis and then just finally emerging as this very different thing. It's... beautiful. For 20 years, our Mobile Tour has traveled across the country, collecting stories from communities nationwide. In 2010, during a stop in Los Angeles, 85-year-old Stella Beltrán sat down with her son and granddaughter to reflect on her childhood journey from Mexico to the U.S. Now 101, Stella returns to StoryCorps with her family to share an update. As heard on NPR's "Morning Edition" on Friday, July 4th, 2025.

Learn more: https://storycorps.org/stories/centenarian-is-a-proud-american/
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] In 2010, 85 year old Stella Beltran (SB) sat down with her son Steven (STB) and granddaughter Mari (MB) to remember moving to the U.S. from Mexico as a small child. SB: We arrived in Texas in 1928. We lived on Leroy Street. It was close to the railroad tracks. When the cars went by, they were loaded with carrots, potatoes, beets. During those years, the men sitting up there would throw things to the people, we would line up and we took a bag. And we'd pick up what they throw. Under the bridge of the track was the hobo. And they had a big kettle of water, and everyone that passed by there was to contribute something, so they could have something to eat also. So we used to clean the pieces of carrot or whatever we got and put it in that kettle for them. My father always said that we were to share what we had, because he had brought us to this country, And this country was going to be very kind to everyone, not just the rich, not just the ones of importance, but everyone. MB: Has this country been kind to you? SB: I really truly believe that this country has been wonderful to me. I remember, I think was in the sixth grade, when they asked me to say my favorite poem. And I said ‘The Star-Spangled Banner.’ I love being here. I love what I thought being a citizen was. MB: What is being a citizen to you? SB: To me, being a citizen is being accountable to what I was raised to believe in: in human beings, in the poor; in the ones that are afraid, in the ones that need help. MB: Are you a citizen? SB: No, I am not. STB: When did you first learn that you weren't a citizen? SB: Oh my goodness... We were going to celebrate our 50th anniversary, and I went to try and get a passport, and that's when I found out. MB: How did you feel? SB: I felt like maybe people feel when they are doused with flame or something. I didn’t know what to do. I'm in the country my father chose for us. I belong here. And I'm going to stay here, and I'm going to do the best that I can and I'm going to represent my father and my mother and myself in the best way possible. [Text] In 2025, Stella and her family sat down for an update. STB: Did you finally get your citizenship? SB: Oh yes! It was big, big, big thing for me. It meant the world. MB: You're about to be 101. SB: Yes, ma'am! SB: I'm looking forward to it because I sit outside and enjoy watching the world go by. I love being here, and I love being me. [Text] Follow us. Twitter. Facebook. Instagram. In 1968, Nathaniel Estes laid the groundwork—and the pipework—for his own plumbing business in Denver’s Five Points neighborhood. As the business grew, so did his reputation as a pillar  in the local Black community. Now 94, Nathaniel still holds a place of honor in the hearts of his children, Eddie Estes and Cathy Lane, who remember the ups, downs, and occasional leaks of life growing up as the plumber’s kids.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en [Text] In 1968, Nathaniel Estes started his own plumbing business in Denver's Five-Points neighborhood. As his company grew, he became a pillar of the local Black community. His son, Eddie Estes (EE), and daughter, Cathy Lane (CL), remember their now 94-year-old father, and what it was like growing up as the plumber’s kids. CL: When I was in the first grade, I said that my father was a plumber. And this little boy said,   "Your father sticks his hands in people's  toilets! Ha-ha-ha!" And he told the whole   class. And I came back with this catch.  "If your daddy made as much as my daddy,   he'd stick his whole head in the toilet." After that, no one teased me and I never was ashamed  that my father was a plumber. EE: I remember when I was 6 years old and I was out for the summer break and Dad told me I had to go  to work. And I told him, "Can Mama go with me?" I'd run and get parts. I was like a plumber's helper. CL: What I remembered is this little seat that would fit on a toilet no matter where you and Daddy was so that you can use the bathroom. So you had that in one hand and Daddy's hand in another hand. I didn't start working until I was eight. It was my job to troubleshoot over the phone. "Good afternoon, Estes Plumbing. May I help you?" And if I took too long of a lunch break, I would get fired. I think I've been fired at least four times by Mommy. She was more serious than any boss  I've ever had. But Mom and Dad made me feel like there was nothing I couldn't get if you work hard for it. I remember Daddy started getting those recognitions from the city. We just seen him rise. I just remember everybody knew him. EE: 'Cause he gave a lot. CL: He gave a lot. EE: When I was a kid, I used to watch him and how he does. So when I was growing up, I wanted to be like him! I'm used to him being my only boss, all my life. Rayford Junior Miles was a World War II veteran from Alabama who could come off as a classic tough guy. But to his granddaughter Melanie Harrison, he was just “Papa.” In 2011, Melanie came to StoryCorps with her father, Jim Miles, to remember the man they both loved — one with a soft heart and a unique way of communicating. More than a decade later, she returned to reflect on her enduring connection with the family members who have passed on. At StoryCorps, Melanie shared what it means to keep their memories alive.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Rayford Junior Miles — a World War II veteran from Alabama — could come off as a classic tough guy. But to his granddaughter Melanie Harrison (MH), he was just ‘Papa.’ At StoryCorps, Melanie sat down with her father, Jim Miles (JM), to remember her grandfather. MH: I remember, I was young enough to be in a high chair. Papa got me out and gave me his chewing tobacco kiss. There were a lot of them, but they were appreciated. JM: His grandmothers taught him to chew when he was like eight years old or something. And my father was an expert at flipping you off. Now he didn't do it out of meanness— just kidding around, he'd shoot you a bird. And if he was really, really on a thing there, he'd shoot two at the same time— bang, bang! And they were crisp, they snapped. It was a work of art. So a couple days before he died, when I was up visiting the hospital, we talked for 15 minutes and I said, ‘Well, we got, we gotta go now.’ And he didn't nod or anything. He just bang, bang, just flipped those birds out. And as we were coming home, I looked into the sky and I saw a cosmic finger. It was a gigantic dark cloud formation, it was a perfect bird. And I said, Mel, look at this. And then you looked at it and you said, ‘Oh my God.’ And you told me today that you think that was just my father's last bird. I'm outta here. MH: I'm done. That was fun. JM: Honest, it was there. It was the clearest cloud formation I've ever seen. MH: Whenever I, I see a big cloudy day, and big storm clouds roll past... I look for 'em . You know, right after he died, I had a dream that I was in the house. And he was just sitting there with his hands across his belly, like he usually did. Just looking at me. Like, y’know, ‘It's cool.’ JM: ‘You'll be okay.’ MH: Yeah. JM: Hm. That’s something to think about. MH: My name is Melanie Harrison. It's been 14 years since I had that conversation with my dad. He passed away in 2019. My dad looked like Santa Claus, and at six foot six, he was a gentle giant. I loved going places with him and letting everybody see like, "oh, that's why she's so tall!" I think when my dad saw the finger in the sky, it helped him process what was upcoming. He may not have shared it was something he was struggling with, but we knew. He knew he would have to step up and help take care of his mom. And all of the changes that come along when a parent dies. And the cloud was like my Papa saying… ‘You’re gonna be all right.’ When my dad passed, I had dreams very similar to the dream that I had of his father, after he passed— he just kind of smiled, and let me know that it was okay. As the years go by, I don't have as many dreams, but both of them pop up in there every now and then. They're little things that help you remember that you're gonna be able to move forward. And it's… it’s always good to see them again. [Text] Follow us. Twitter. Facebook. Instagram. And watch more on YouTube. [Logo] StoryCorps. [Logo] Corporation for Public Broadcasting. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US JEFF: I don't know a lot of people that called him Leonard. Everyone called him Mat. I met him at a Thanksgiving dinner. We were sitting in the living room and we were watching Macy's Day Parade on Thanksgiving Day. He didn't say too much at all until, um, someone started saying, "Mat, what are you up to?" And that's when Mat opened up. He said, "Well, you know they're looking for a candidate to challenge the gays in the military laws. They're looking for an officer preferably someone who has a good record to make it legal to be in the service and be open. I've got these awards from the service, I think I can do it." I think even the NBC and the CBS news put that cover on their TV that night. And when he called, all I could do was tell him how proud I was of him. And then I didn't hear from him for a while. And, he died of AIDS. He was young, 44 years old. I didn't even know he was sick. Before he died, he was discharged. He lost everything, you know. No benefits, no nothing. He was buried in DC, and uh, his headstone does not have his name on it. It strictly says "A gay Vietnam veteran," And, uh, the inscription on it is, "When I was in the military, they gave me a medal for killing two men and a discharge for loving one." He, he was the epitome of a perfect soldier, one of those people that stuck his neck out. And he was proud to be the person to challenge that law.

On The TODAY Show, Tony Goldwyn, Octavia Spencer and Jenna Bush Hager shared something that feels rare on national television: hope. They sat down to discuss Tony’s experiences with One Small Step, a project from StoryCorps that brings people with different political beliefs together for one respectful, face-to-face conversation.

They believe, like we do, that real conversations, even with people we disagree with, can change hearts, build bridges, and remind us of our shared humanity.

It can be so powerful to show up and care when it feels easier to walk away, and to see what happens when we swap assumptions for real conversation.

We don’t have to agree on everything to start seeing each other more clearly. And it doesn’t take a sweeping act, just one step.

What happens when a progressive LGBTQ+ news creator and a Christian leadership coach sit down to talk, not debate?
Brenda Cox Harkins and V Spehar (Under The Desk News) took One Small Step to prove that our differences don’t have to lead to a disconnect.
They talked about faith, identity, belonging, and what it means to show up even when it’s hard. 
They laughed. They got quiet. They asked brave questions without easy answers.
And somewhere in the conversation, they found a connection not in spite of their differences but because of them.
Their honest, thoughtful conversation is a reminder:

We’re all more than a label.

You don’t have to agree to care.

Every person has a story worth hearing.
This is the kind of conversation that reminds us: bridging divides isn’t just a one-time thing.

Who in your life needs to see what listening without judgment looks like?
