BRENDA HARKINS: I think that there's a sense that, um, I like to provide a safe environment for people, and I'd love for people to know they're loved. And one of the things I do even in business is, um, help teams figure out the differences within the team that helps them to be, uh, better who they are together. And so I think that's just what I've done in life, all of my life. I look at the awesomeness about people and I draw it out. I love to mine the gold in people. That's what I really love to do, because I believe every single one of us has treasure inside of us. And so I think when, when people do that with you, you know, like if somebody comes up to you and they're, they, they genuinely love you, you feel the authenticity and you feel the safeness and they're calling out what's great about you. I mean, who doesn't wanna be in a relationship with that? I do. You know? V SPEHAR: Do you think it's difficult to. Interact with other folks, you know, in Texas, right? Which has some really strict right-wing laws, um, or within the church or within your community who maybe aren't as welcoming as you. Like, how do you navigate that space? BRENDA HARKINS: Well, I've got people who don't like me on all sides. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: And I've got people who do on all sides. So, you know, it's a win-win. Um, there are, um, people who have strong convictions that political issues are spiritual issues, and I disagree with that. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: And so that has not made me some friends within the church world. Um... and then I've had some challenges with others who, um... I have friends, I have family who are in relationships that are gay, relationships that are married, that are, and I love them dearly. And we're friends and we — and we're family too, by the way. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Um, and so... You know, a lot of times they wish that I would stand up and speak out for who they are and what, and I'm like, "Well, those are your convictions and that's for you to stand up and speak out for. I'll stand up for you 'cause I love you, but you know: you are the one that stands up for your convictions, and I'll stand up for mine, and we'll stand up for each other in relationship and love each other really well through all the differences. So I don't know if that answered your question or not. V SPEHAR: Yeah, it surely does. I think a lot though about the crossover between major political movements and the idea of religious broadly. Right? So like when we think about the women's suffrage movement, a lot of that came out of, um, the Quakers of, uh, Western New York. Or when we think about the civil rights movement, Dr. King was a Baptist preacher. I do think there is like a big crossover between politics and religion when it comes to advancing humanity that a lot of folks, um... I think rightly right now, feel stuck up against, because there's not like the establishment that's so clear. And then the counter movement, maybe the way there was in like the sixties and seventies, and now it's kind of like, um, you know, you might look at some of the stuff that, let's say... Donald Trump does and say, um, "Well, is that in line with a counter movement that perpetuates humanity? Is that in line with Christian values or can we pick and choose? Can we separate the art from the artist?" And for me, sometimes it's, no, we can't separate, um, you know, some of the convictions that somebody has when it comes to politics from the way they claim to be religiously. BRENDA HARKINS: No, I totally agree. I, I agree with that. I agree a hundred percent with that. V SPEHAR: What do you think influenced your, like, personal political beliefs the most? Like did you have a moment as an adult where you were like, "Hey, I think this is where I'm going, this is where I feel I most fit in"? BRENDA HARKINS: Well, first of all, I'm not a terribly political person. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: I'm more of a... I love, uh, faith, family, friends, west Texas sunsets, and great coffee. I mean, I love that, you know, and, um, and the other issues, I do... I vote of course, right? But I'm just not a political activist. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: And I'd love to hear more about you on that subject, but I think that for my personal beliefs, what influenced me the most is probably my dad, who actually, for a lot of my — from 12 to 18, we didn't even speak. V SPEHAR: Mmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Um, but the years before and the years that were restored after, um, helped me see who he was and, um... he was, he was someone who grew up extreme — in extreme poverty, who was given a pair of shoes by a dentist and decided when he grew up he was gonna be a dentist. And he did. And you know, he just, uh, he put his mind to things and he did them, and he loved people so big, uh, in all walks of life. And I think that that probably personally has been what has influenced me the most. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah, please tell me about you. I would love to know — personally or politically or both, right? I would love to know about you. V SPEHAR: So for me, unfortunately, like my mere existence is political now, right? Everybody has an idea about gay people, what rights they should or shouldn't have, what type of inherent rights their marriages should or shouldn't have. So every single day I don't get the sort of like option to opt out of, of being political because my very existence has been made political. Um, I got my early ideas about politics from my dad who was a military contractor, and we come from a deeply patriotic military-type family, and I... you know, was little during the Desert Storm wars, and it was my first week in college in New York City when 9/11 happened. And so I have had this like very front-row seat to what patriotism from the 90s and early 2000s was, versus what it's become now. Um, and I still believe myself to be a deeply patriotic person. I mean, like, this is my office, right? Like it's very... BRENDA HARKINS: I love it. I love it so much. V SPEHAR: It's very that way, you know? Um, and I think I tend to look at political figures as deeply human figures and not these like, you know, uh, folks up on a pedestal who were omnipotent and they knew everything. I'm like... I don't think so. I think they were human people making human decisions a lot of the time. And that brings me a lot of peace. I started off as a Republican, which I had to explain to Obama one time to his face when we were making a TikTok together. And he was like, "Well, you voted for me, right?" And I was like, "Uh, no sir. I — I was like 19 and my dad took me and we voted for, of course, John McCain, 'cause that was, like, my dad's hero-type person." And then the next time I was working for Mitt Romney as a caterer for the 2012 RNC. And I just really thought he was great because when he was governor of Massachusetts, he was the first governor to sign in gay marriage. And that was like, I was a single-issue voter. I wanted to vote at, I think it was like 20... well, what was it, like 25 at that time or something? That I really wanted gay marriage to be legal. And um, so we, so we did that. And uh, I voted for Romney. And I remember being backstage one time, and this is when I sort of switched from Republican to Democrat. Um, and Romney was asking the catering staff like, "Are you gonna vote for me?" And I was like, "Yes." And I told him because of the gay marriage thing. And he was like, "Yeah, that was — I don't know why people are so bothered, why they wanna be involved in other people's bedrooms. That's just not something I wanna spend my eight years dealing with, so I'm — I don't wanna deal with it." I thought that was great. And then he went on stage and he said the exact opposite, right? 'Cause he had to kind of appease the Tea Party and I was devastated because I'd really believed him. Um, and then, you know, you start to learn from politics how they all play the game behind the scenes. And then I changed to be a Democrat when in 20... um... 15, that we got gay marriage through the Obergefell decision. And I just felt more aligned with that party because they had shown me the action that I had so desperately wanted. Um... I think that there are issues in the Democratic Party just the same as there were in the Republican Party, and I think that they benefit greatly, both sides, from... That's why I wanted to do this, Brenda, because they benefit so greatly from being like, "Brenda and V will never talk. Nope. They would tear each other's hair out. There could never ever be a time in which these people could find common ground. And we already have like five times now, right? So... BRENDA HARKINS: Right. V SPEHAR: That's what I think is interesting about politics. Um, and I think the "all or nothing of it" has become so pervasive to folks that there's gonna be people who watch my show who are gonna be like, "I can't believe you went on there and risked potentially talking to somebody who we don't agree with." And I'm like, "I know. Uh. I also had Marianne Williamson on this morning, so you know, we go, we go all over the place over here." BRENDA HARKINS: Well, I think if we don't talk to people who don't agree with us, that we never grow, if all we do is surround ourself with people who have the same position, also there's no influence. You just have a bunch of cheerleaders around you with, you know, like what influence is there if people already agree with you? Like, let's build some bridges and, and get a bigger perspective on all of this. By the way, you did say that you came from a patriotic family. Mm-hmm. And I wanna ask you what that means to you. Like what is patriotism to you? V SPEHAR: It's a lot of things. So in particular, it's like... my dad's a really good singer and he used to, like, anytime we would have a problem, he'd take us for rides in the Jeep, which would inevitably end with him singing "Proud to be an American" or something from Lee Greenwood at the end. And 'cause he was, but he had this idea that men in particular are only allowed a certain avenues to release their emotions. And that was like, when you love a woman or love your country, those are the only two times that you can be in any way sort of like... exuberant about the way you feel. And so, um, I learned a lot from him about patriotism. Um, and I also learned the difference between like patriotism and national pride and how those things can be different. You can believe in your country and want the best for it, and also, uh, be able to point out when somebody's not doing the right thing for it, and not just be so beholden to a personality or a politician that you don't put country first. And I think putting country first oftentimes means putting people first. And this is where I could get a little bit, uh, you know, into it with the Republican side who, um, sometimes thinks things like Medicaid or SNAP benefits or the way that we provide aid to other countries isn't putting America first. But to me, I always liked being the hero. Like my whole lens has been from the idea that, like going back to my grandparents, right? Um, when people who were in these concentration camps heard American voices, they knew that they were saved, right? That was the end. When you hear American voices, you should feel safe. And so that's my perspective on politics and patriotism, and that's what I hope to continue to perpetuate. And I worry nowadays that sometimes when they hear American voices here or abroad that they don't feel safe anymore. BRENDA HARKINS: Mmm. That's good. V SPEHAR: What about you? BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah, well, patriotism, a lot of that goes back to my dad as well. He was... V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: You know, he was extremely patriotic. I remember the songs, I remember all of that. I remember tears in his eyes, which I never saw that I would see... V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: ...was singing those songs. And, um, and I guess to me it means, um. Loving your coun — country, but not to the... well, I don't think love is ever being blind to the faults of it. So loving your country and in, in the way that you see, um, you can help make it better to do that. I, I actually think this that we're doing is one of those ways. V SPEHAR: So from this conversation, I know I'm gonna like, you know, call my wife and my friends and be like, "I met the most lovely lady from Texas today." How will having a conversation with me sort of like change the way you feel maybe about the way that religion and politics intersect, or about the way we reach out to people? BRENDA HARKINS: I think more than change it, it will affirm the importance of it, V. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: I feel like, um, I feel like I'd love to sit down and have a cup of coffee with you when we're not being recorded, and I just... V SPEHAR: I know. Well, you can, they'll give you my phone number. They have it. BRENDA HARKINS: Okay. V SPEHAR: I talk to people all day. That's my job. BRENDA HARKINS: No, I, I would love, um, yeah, I would love to get to know you better. And I feel like that is one of the things that... I mean, you have affirmed that to me today, because I didn't know. I never know when I get on one of these conversations how it's gonna go and... it's another person that's a beautiful human that has a lot of gold inside of 'em, and I've seen that today, and I appreciate that, and I thank you for like... sharing so much of who you are with me today. So, I don't know, does that answer your question? V SPEHAR: Yes, absolutely. Um, my other, my other question is, you know, we talked about first impressions when we read each other's bio, but when my background came up, right, and knowing just what you knew about me, was any of this a surprise to you that this is like the kind of stuff that I would — someone with my bio surrounds themself with? BRENDA HARKINS: Oh no, but you know what, it wasn't a surprise to me. I loved it that I saw Lincoln back there. I love your smiley cup and that eagle — I will have to take a picture and send you my, the, the door knocker on my... V SPEHAR: Oh, right on. BRENDA HARKINS: ...looks almost exactly like that. V SPEHAR: Yeah. BRENDA HARKINS: And it was on my husband's great-great-grandfather's house or something like that, so. V SPEHAR: Wow. BRENDA HARKINS: Um, I'm like, "Wow! Already we have an eagle in common, you know?" V SPEHAR: I know! BRENDA HARKINS: Um, so no, it didn't surprise me 'cause I didn't really have any... I don't, I ne — I don't ever really have any preconceived ideas. My main concern is that we connect. V SPEHAR: Right, right. BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah. V SPEHAR: So of all the kids that you have, do they share your political and religious beliefs too? BRENDA HARKINS: Oh goodness, no! Goodness no. V SPEHAR: No, they don't? How do you handle that? BRENDA HARKINS: No, not all of them, my goodness. Um, so we've got — so I had three, my husband had two when we got married. We've had two together. We have 12 grandchildren. I have one great-grandbaby. I cannot believe that. That's ridiculous... V SPEHAR: Wow! BRENDA HARKINS: ...And wonderful. Ridiculous, and wonderful. Um. So, yeah, we've got all different perspectives, like from... way far left to way far right. And Thanksgiving is fun. Now, we, we do love each other and we, um — for a lot of our gatherings, we just choose to leave those differences out and love each other and have fun together. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Um, and then some of them like to... blow up things by dropping a bomb and seeing what'll happen, you know? So, um... V SPEHAR: How do you navigate that? Like when there is a disagreement with people, you know, at the holiday? BRENDA HARKINS: I listen and I ask questions. V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah. I, I listen for what... I li — I usually try to listen for why they did it, um, why they started it. And then I ask what's important to them about that. And then I really listen 'cause I really care. V SPEHAR: Mmm. BRENDA HARKINS: I really do. I mean, I may not agree, but they may s — sway me, you know? Like... I'm not so grounded in where I'm at that I, I don't look at other perspectives and, and incorporate that into who I am. So... V SPEHAR: Is there any like example you could give of, sometime you think somebody, like, dropped a bomb and how you guys got through it? BRENDA HARKINS: Oh, I hate those spur-of-the-moment questions and I've gotta think of... V SPEHAR: I know. BRENDA HARKINS: Um... let me be thinking about it while I ask you, okay? V SPEHAR: Sure! BRENDA HARKINS: I'll be, be trying to think about that. But — how do you navigate disagreements? Like, do you have that within your family? It sounds like you might from the background, and how do you navigate that? V SPEHAR: So my family — um, I, I feel like... used to fight more when I was younger. My mom had the energy for it. Now we don't. Um, there's a lot of like, "We just don't see those people anymore. We just don't choose to have those fights anymore." And on the other side, on my wife's family, we've been "no contact" with her parents for quite some time. And that came after years and years and years and years of begging them to... show up with kindness or tolerance at a minimum, and their continued commitment to make themself the victim of like, having to endure being at an event with my gay marriage to their daughter, that they didn't necessarily fully understand, that they constantly wanted to question, that they constantly wanted to question her... Um, and it just got to a point where it... Honestly, it's like one of the greatest heartbreaks, the most difficult thing I think a lot of people think going "no contact" will be easier. And it's not. BRENDA HARKINS: No. V SPEHAR: It is the greatest, perpetual, constant reoccurring grief that a family can go through and to have it go on for so long without the other side breaking is just... Brenda, like... the hardest thing because like, we don't have children, but we want them soon. And I can't imagine if my child said to me, "You've hurt me so gravely that I need to take space from you," that I wouldn't give them the space and then like, I don't know, camp out on their lawn to be like, "I'm so sorry. I'll do anything to like — to like — please, I, it's me. I, I will take all the blame, like I just can't live like this." But to, to be sort of like continually rejected, um, is very difficult. So that's how... BRENDA HARKINS: Yes. V SPEHAR: ...our holidays sometimes go. A lot of tears. A lot of tears in a "no-contact" family. When you think that you'll get relief, each time you think, "Well, this time it won't be as bad," and every time it's really hard. BRENDA HARKINS: Wow. I'm so sorry for that. V SPEHAR: Mmm. BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah. The, the separation, the closing people out: that's "the loud," that is "the loud," the, there is so much loudness in that silence right there, in that separation. There's so much that's just screaming. Um, it... hmm. V SPEHAR: And it comes down to people's allegiance, right? Like, will you, will, in this case, will you decide that your allegiance is to the president — um, whether he's actively the president at that moment or not — or to your child? And I think it's really difficult for some people, and I, I do wonder how they get to that point, and why it's so hard seemingly to come back from it to say that, like, their allegiance to a president, um, and that person's very far right ideals, supersedes their ability to love their child anymore. That's something that I, I have like a really difficult time understanding or finding space for, which is how you end up "no contact," because it's like, "How many more ways can I ask you to love me?" Right? Or in this case, my wife asked her parents to love her and to keep — be continually rejected until she comes around, and it's like, "Comes around to what? The man wants to get rid of gay marriage by June. How am I gonna come around to that? It seems like maybe you guys gotta come around a little bit this way and maybe we're — find a closer middle." But for a lot of families that just hasn't happened. BRENDA HARKINS: Well, and that's where when you have issues that become more important than loving relationships, it's, uh... it's heartbreaking, it's devastating, and... V SPEHAR: Mm-hmm. Is that something — you'd never let that happen with your kids? BRENDA HARKINS: No. V SPEHAR: Yeah. BRENDA HARKINS: No. V SPEHAR: Are we getting an invite to Christmas, Brenda? I feel like... BRENDA HARKINS: Come to Texas for Christmas! Oh my gosh, that would be so fun. V SPEHAR: You just picked up two more, right? BRENDA HARKINS: Maybe we'll do that. V SPEHAR: It has been such a treat to chat. BRENDA HARKINS: I mean, you're welcome! I will say that! V SPEHAR: So what has surprised you from this chat now that we're at the end of our chat? BRENDA HARKINS: Um, that — well that I haven't asked more questions. You've been talking and asking me and I haven't asked you nearly enough and I wanna hear more. Um... What has surprised me? I think what has delighted me is a better word, is that, um, that you seem like a delightful person. That you seem like a very caring person and, um... and that, that makes me very happy. I am, I, I, I am delighted that I feel that there was a connection here, and I hope it will continue. V SPEHAR: Absolutely. BRENDA HARKINS: What about you? What have you — what surprised you? V SPEHAR: I gotta tell you, it might be, it might be like another arrow in the quiver today to be like, I'm — this nice lady Brenda, who has, you know, fairly conservative and Jesus-forward values also understands that you don't abandon your children for a president. So I feel like I've got one more example of not being crazy, and that is a huge gift to me because sometimes you can feel so alone, with not knowing that many people who you think are on the opposite side of the aisle of you — be that for religion or politics or just like lifestyle or anything, um — but there are these universal truths that we need to continue to remind each other of, which are like, no, you love your family more than anything, and your children more than anything. And politics comes and goes, and what we wanna do is make sure that we're presenting, like, the best, safest America. We all — both agreed on that. Um... BRENDA HARKINS: Yes we did. V SPEHAR: And so I feel, I feel really, um... sort of like, lightened by that — that, you know, the times in which we see so much hate online, or we see so much resistance and grief in our real lives are maybe — maybe there's not as much more of that out there. Uh, and maybe there's a lot more good out there and we should be trying to build that together as a society, as opposed to trying to assume that everybody is, um, you know, as hateful as the most hateful person we've ever met. BRENDA HARKINS: Yes! I think that there — I think we honestly do have so much more. People in general have so much more in common than they have different, and we just need to take the time to talk about these things instead of keeping that "us and them" mentality. Um, let's get to know each other before we make those assumptions, so. V SPEHAR: Well, that's it for me and Brenda, who are starting a new podcast next week where we help you with your family! Thank you very much, Brenda; it's been a pleasure to get to chat with you, um, and your family's very lucky to have you. You just seem like such a, a bright light, um, keeping everybody together, and that's just, that's what we need out here. More of that. BRENDA HARKINS: Oh, it's been a joy to meet you, and I look forward to connecting with you again! V SPEHAR: Yeah, absolutely. BRENDA HARKINS: Yeah. Yeah. Okay. Well, all the best to you. V SPEHAR: You too. BRENDA HARKINS: Bye-bye. See you Christmas. V SPEHAR: Yes. See you at Christmas and uh, you know, I might give you my mother-in-law's phone number... Give her a little call. Be like, "Hey, woman-to-woman, in the peer group. Knock it off." BRENDA HARKINS: Okay, we'll see you. Bye-bye.

After experiencing a bout of postpartum depression, Kalvin Bridgewater started the Daddy Stroller Social Club, a supportive community for other fathers. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] Kalvin Bridgewater (KB) started the Daddy Stroller Social Club in Fort Worth, Texas after his bout with postpartum depression. The club has become a way for dads to support each other. He came to StoryCorps with Landon Taylor (LT) – a club member turned-close friend – to talk about when he first became a father. KB: I didn't know how to be a dad. I was like, “Man, what, what am I doing?” Driving home, leaving that birth center… I felt like I just needed to hold everything together. But, looking at my wife, she had these communities for moms to just open up and share with each other. LT: I had the same experience. My wife had an IVF group And I remember seeing the five of them sharing tears, just hug. KB: I think all dads need a space where we could show some vulnerability. LT: Mm-hmm. KB: So I hit up some of my friends. There was maybe three or four of us, took the kids to the park and let them play. And then, we went from five to 10 dads to maybe 15 dads to then 300 plus. But, I get a phone call that my baby brother got rushed to the hospital. LT: Mmm. Um, he ended up, um, passing away. And, I was like, “Yep, like I gotta climb in my black hole.” LT: Mmm. KB: I told the guys what happened. Didn't tell 'em where we was gonna have the funeral at or what time it was gonna be... And, as I'm going through his funeral and I look up and I see all these dads from the park, you know, in the audience. And I'm like, “What are these guys doing down here?” And they was like, “Man, we gonna ride with you. We gonna make sure you okay.” I said, “Man, these, these guys are stuck on me for life.” LB: Wow, man, I am, uh, tearing up with you, man. You are stuck with me. I don’t follow a lot of people easily, but for you, I will always be a student of you, my brother. KB: What’s something that surprised you about becoming a father? LT: I'm probably more emotional now than ever. I think you probably can say the same, man. You know, my father was my biggest cheerleader. He passed away, and he never had a chance to see, you know, me have my child. But, I'm able to see him in my son. KB: And I know your dad is looking down on you like, “Well done.” I'm thankful every day that I know you. You know, every time we get off the phone, first thing I tell you, man, is “I love you.” Because I want you to understand that. LB: And I'm here to tell you in front of the entire world that you are not alone. Um, so, never feel like your burden is ever too heavy for us. We have you. [Text] Follow us. Twitter. Facebook. What happens when you sit down with someone you’ve been told you’ll never understand?
Liberal actor and activist Tony Goldwyn and conservative nonprofit leader and father Ben Sauceda couldn’t come from more different political worlds.

But, in their One Small Step conversation, they demonstrate something many of us are craving right now: how to stay open, stay curious, and make space for shared humanity, even when you disagree. 

In a time when it feels easier to retreat into our corners, this conversation shows us what’s possible when we step outside of them.

Know someone who believes in bridging divides through conversation? This is the one to send their way.

Then ask yourself: who might surprise you if you gave them a chance to speak?

BEN SAUCEDA: Thank you. JONATHAN Z: Welcome! TONY GOLDWYN: A treat... BEN SAUCEDA: Yes, thank you. TONY GOLDWYN: ...to get to do this, yeah. BEN SAUCEDA: I'm excited about this. TONY GOLDWYN: Me too. I hope to have an interesting conversation to make contact with someone I don't know. I don't really have any fears, uh... except that I don't have any idea where this conversation's headed, but that's always exciting. BEN SAUCEDA: My name is Ben Sauceda, I am 41, and I'm here in New York City with Tony Goldwyn, who is my One Small Step partner today. TONY GOLDWYN: Ben, um, was born and raised in Wichita, Kansas, firstborn to a first-generation American Hispanic family, and is the CEO of a prominent nonprofit in Wichita. BEN SAUCEDA: And this is Tony's bio: he's been married to his wife Jane for almost 38 years — that's incredible — and has two daughters, Anna and Tess. Tony grew up in Los Angeles, uh, but has lived in the tri-state since college. Uh, Tony is an actor and director in the entertainment industry. TONY GOLDWYN: Okay, so first question is: Ben, why did you sign up for One Small Step? BEN SAUCEDA: So, for me it was really important to have dialogue and conversations with people who, who have different opinions and beliefs than I do. TONY GOLDWYN: It is so important for me to, to... have con — be in conversation with people, particularly people who might look at the world in a different way than I do, to challenge myself to listen and see another perspective. And, um, I'm very concerned in our country today and in our society in general, for many, many reasons, we've stopped listening to each other, and stopped learning how to talk to each other, and people are afraid to talk to each other. BEN SAUCEDA: There are extremes on both sides, no doubt, that don't have the same end goal. But I would say you could probably say that 80% of Americans have the same end goal. Just the avenues in which we're getting there looks different. So how do or did your politics and general beliefs, um, differ from your parents or your family? TONY GOLDWYN: My father was actually a Republican for much of my life. BEN SAUCEDA: Okay. TONY GOLDWYN: But my mom and my stepfather were very — you know, ardent and sometimes strident Democrats. Uh, and I grew up through Watergate and all that as a seminal kind of experience. It was about, you know, uh, when I started to be awakening to politics and when I was a small kid, the Vietnam War. And, and, and so there was a, it was a very, um, politically tumultuous time when I was a young kid. So we had a lot of very spirited, um, conversations around the dinner tables in, in my family. BEN SAUCEDA: Interestingly enough, my parents were not political. So I will say as a second-generation Hispanic involved in the Hispanic community back home, yes, it is assumed that I should be a liberal Democrat. My mom leans conservative. Uh, my dad is kind of indifferent and I — my dad didn't register to vote till 2012 or 2010. Um, and he's only voted I think three times. Uh, twice was when I ran for office, and so he had to vote for me. Like, "That was kind of the deal, Dad!" TONY GOLDWYN: Ben, is there something that gives you hope for the future? I'm guessing talking to you that there's a lot that gives you hope for the future! BEN SAUCEDA: There is a lot. So again, for me, faith is such a central part of my life. I, I've grown up that way, but I — it's, it's become personal and real for me. And so to that degree, my faith is truly what gives me hope. What about for you? What, what... TONY GOLDWYN: I, I feel exactly the same way. Faith is a big one and it's, um — uh, I'm not formally religious, I was not raised in a religious tradition, but I have tremendous faith in humanity. BEN SAUCEDA: Yeah. TONY GOLDWYN: And, uh, that, that is a deeply spiritual dimension for me. I know that when people put down, put aside their assumptions about other people and just talk, the miracles happen. I, I feel that we all need to, um, take responsibility for that. And so I have a, I have a lot of faith that, um, most people, uh, crave that. BEN SAUCEDA: Yeah. Yeah, I agree. I think the more that we talk and the more that you just have these conversations, people realize that we have a lot more in common than what divides us. TONY GOLDWYN: Yeah. Look, it's why I do what I do for a living. I mean, I'm a storyteller for a living, and I've seen the impact of when you tell stories, that completely transcends politics and presumption. You see, you get inside other people's lives and experience their experience in a subjective way, and it changes you. BEN SAUCEDA: Yeah. TONY GOLDWYN: Um. And um, and people who relate to the — who, maybe you're telling a story that's related to their life, they feel seen. That's what we all want: to see and be seen. BEN SAUCEDA: Exactly. Exactly. I appreciate this. This has been fantastic. TONY GOLDWYN: Yeah, likewise. Likewise. BEN SAUCEDA: Yeah. I think one of the things I learned today about Tony was just: I've always had preconceived notions going to that there about someone in the film industry. Tony's just a great down-to-earth individual that you could have a great conversation with, really. Uh, it was something I took away from today. TONY GOLDWYN: My conversation with Ben really, um, confirmed for me my belief and, and strong instinct that people are so multifaceted and complex that the things that di — where we differ is a beautiful thing. It's... like that's, that's a positive, um, to interact with people who, who are — have different beliefs from different cultures, a different worldview, uh, um... And you'll inevitably find that there are endless similarities as well.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] In 2020, Ingrid Hoch (IH) and Brian Lahr (BL) were hired as managers on a big construction project: creating a brand new terminal at the San Diego International Airport. But before the job had officially begun, COVID hit. Ingrid and Brian had to find ways to keep morale up in the middle of the pandemic. At StoryCorps, they remembered how some tiny insects helped them do just that. IH: When I came back to work in person, it was still masks, it was still distance. And so we planted a vegetable garden that would bring us together. And in early summer, we started to notice that there were four caterpillars. BL: And they kept getting bigger and bigger, and once word got out, people were like, ‘Hey, hey check out the caterpillars.’ I mean, you got guys who are walking around with hard hats, looking at these little four caterpillars every day. IH: Workers go out there and they're just like, ‘You know what? I just feel more at peace when I'm watching these things.’ Soon enough all the little guys make their chrysalis. And it's a beautiful lime green cocoon, but then within 24 hours, they turn translucent. BL: And your first thought is ‘Oh, crap, it died.’ But, you stare at it and then they start coming out. It's crazy. So then I said, ‘Why don't we just make the whole thing into a monarch butterfly enclosure type thing?’ We got some of the toughest guys you've ever seen working out there in the field, the next thing you know, they're saying, ‘When are you gonna release the butterflies?’ The day we did their big release party, probably over a hundred people come to watch us. IH: We thought there'd be a flurry of butterflies that just explode but they do not do that, they're like, more cautious. People came down, we're like, ‘If you wanna like let one get on your finger,’ and then, it's the most delicate touch of those little legs. And there was such joy and so many smiles. That next year we had 120 monarchs. And then last year we had 350 monarchs. And this year we're hoping for 600 plus. BL: So what is it you wanna take away from the job when you leave? IH: That I cared about the people. I know the job, that's why we're here. But I think getting something done is not the point of living. And, we will all be transformed, those who worked on this project. We can look at that transformation that butterflies go through: from an egg to caterpillar to that chrysalis and then just finally emerging as this very different thing. It's... beautiful. For 20 years, our Mobile Tour has traveled across the country, collecting stories from communities nationwide. In 2010, during a stop in Los Angeles, 85-year-old Stella Beltrán sat down with her son and granddaughter to reflect on her childhood journey from Mexico to the U.S. Now 101, Stella returns to StoryCorps with her family to share an update. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] In 2010, 85 year old Stella Beltran (SB) sat down with her son Steven (STB) and granddaughter Mari (MB) to remember moving to the U.S. from Mexico as a small child. SB: We arrived in Texas in 1928. We lived on Leroy Street. It was close to the railroad tracks. When the cars went by, they were loaded with carrots, potatoes, beets. During those years, the men sitting up there would throw things to the people, we would line up and we took a bag. And we'd pick up what they throw. Under the bridge of the track was the hobo. And they had a big kettle of water, and everyone that passed by there was to contribute something, so they could have something to eat also. So we used to clean the pieces of carrot or whatever we got and put it in that kettle for them. My father always said that we were to share what we had, because he had brought us to this country, And this country was going to be very kind to everyone, not just the rich, not just the ones of importance, but everyone. MB: Has this country been kind to you? SB: I really truly believe that this country has been wonderful to me. I remember, I think was in the sixth grade, when they asked me to say my favorite poem. And I said ‘The Star-Spangled Banner.’ I love being here. I love what I thought being a citizen was. MB: What is being a citizen to you? SB: To me, being a citizen is being accountable to what I was raised to believe in: in human beings, in the poor; in the ones that are afraid, in the ones that need help. MB: Are you a citizen? SB: No, I am not. STB: When did you first learn that you weren't a citizen? SB: Oh my goodness... We were going to celebrate our 50th anniversary, and I went to try and get a passport, and that's when I found out. MB: How did you feel? SB: I felt like maybe people feel when they are doused with flame or something. I didn’t know what to do. I'm in the country my father chose for us. I belong here. And I'm going to stay here, and I'm going to do the best that I can and I'm going to represent my father and my mother and myself in the best way possible. [Text] In 2025, Stella and her family sat down for an update. STB: Did you finally get your citizenship? SB: Oh yes! It was big, big, big thing for me. It meant the world. MB: You're about to be 101. SB: Yes, ma'am! SB: I'm looking forward to it because I sit outside and enjoy watching the world go by. I love being here, and I love being me. [Text] Follow us. Twitter. Facebook. Instagram. Patrice Hudson wasn’t sure online dating was for her — until she met Byron Ball, a fellow single parent and former spouse who taught high school science. He had a passion for gardening and poured that love into the yard outside her home, which she had no time for. At StoryCorps, she reflected on the quiet legacy he left behind — and how it continues to remind her that love never truly disappears.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en In his profile, we kind of had a dad bod, but I have a mom bod. And when you look deeper in the eyes behind the expression, that's where the handsome is. He had the warmest smile and really beautiful eyes. And he was very handsome. We talked every night on the phone. He was funny and sensitive. and he loved gardening. As a single mom, I did not have time for gardening. I think it pained him to see the status of my backyard. He was very kind about it. He never criticized me, but he did ask if he could plant things for me. Over time, he did a little more and more in the yard to make it pretty. He often did things to show he cared without being asked. But he was diagnosed with cancer eight years after we met. We married in his backyard garden. And about 9 weeks after we married, he passed away. That winter, the house felt big and empty. You know, I didn't feel much like Thanksgiving. I didn't want a Christmas tree. That year felt gray and somber. That spring one morning I realized, "Oh, there were little tulips popping up in a corner of my yard. They were a very rich, lovely purple." Byron knew that purple was my favorite color, so he planted those flowers. He knew he wouldn't live to see them bloom. I could not hold in the tears because with every ounce of my being, I knew that I was loved. That it didn't die with him. He wanted me to know that I did take up gardening. When I'm in the garden, I have had a few tears, but mostly it's joyful. I think that's what Byron would have wanted. He understood that life goes on without him and that's okay. He showed me beyond his grave that he loved me. [Music]

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US Text: Like Brothers Growing up as the youngest in a tight knit family, Barry Romo wasn’t much older than his niece and nephews. He was especially close with his nephew, Robert, who everyone called Bobby. They came of age during the Vietnam War. Barry Romo: Bobby was one month younger than me and we were raised like brothers. I enlisted in the Army to go to Vietnam, that was my intention, And he didn't want to go in the military, but he got drafted anyway. They sent him to Vietnam, and he ended up being in my brigade. I became a lieutenant and he begged me to help him get out of the field. But, I couldn't help him. And, my nephew got me out of Vietnam. One day I got back from a patrol. They told me, “Your nephew Robert has been killed.” He was running to save a friend of his who had been wounded in battle and he was shot in the throat. Enemy fire was too intense. So, they couldn't retrieve the body and he was in the sun for 48 hours. A staff sergeant said, “Why don't we seal the body permanently. That way your family, they’ll remember him as he looked like when he graduated from high school. I was then sent to escort the body home. I had white gloves on, and a uniform with my medals, but I felt dirty, You know, I thought I was gonna die in Vietnam, But, I didn't have to go back there. I had my ticket punched by my nephew's blood. And I felt that I failed him, I failed my family. And, I still feel guilty to this day. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] Chad Machado (CM) and his son, Xavier (XM), live in Kekaha—a small town on Hawaii's western island of Kaua'i. When Chad lost his job during the Covid-19 pandemic, they decided to take a risk and open up a pizza shop. Neither had ever worked in a restaurant before. But I couldn't get you away from the kitchen. XM: You have to eat a lot in order to learn how to cook, you know? CM: Right, right. XM: So I did a lot of eating back when I was a kid. CM: Yeah. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] Kalvin Bridgewater (KB) started the Daddy Stroller Social Club in Fort Worth, Texas after his bout with postpartum depression. The club has become a way for dads to support each other. He came to StoryCorps with Landon Taylor (LT) – a club member turned-close friend – to talk about when he first became a father. KB: I didn't know how to be a dad. I was like, “Man, what, what am I doing?” Driving home, leaving that birth center… I felt like I just needed to hold everything together. But, I get a phone call that my baby brother got rushed to the hospital. LT: Mmm. Um, he ended up, um, passing away. And, I was like, “Yep, like I gotta climb in my black hole.” LT: Mmm. KB: I told the guys what happened. Didn't tell 'em where we was gonna have the funeral at or what time it was gonna be... And, as I'm going through his funeral and I look up and I see all these dads from the park, you know, in the audience. Dan Bigley’s life changed in 2003 when he was mauled by a grizzly bear while fishing on Alaska’s Kenai River. He survived the attack but woke from a 12-day coma to find he had lost his sight. The outdoor activities that once shaped his life were no longer possible, and he faced uncertainty about his future—whether he’d find fulfilling work, build relationships, or have a family. At StoryCorps, Dan spoke with his daughter, Acacia, about how he learned to imagine a new future for himself.

Our Story of the Week, as heard on NPR's Morning Edition on Friday, April 25, 2025.

https://storycorps.org/stories/survived-bear-attack/
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] Fifteen year old Acacia Bigley brought her father Dan to StoryCorps in Anchorage, Alaska to hear how he became blind. Before Acacia was born, Dan was on a fishing trip when he was attacked by a grizzly bear after he accidentally came between her and her cubs. Dan Bigley: She drug me off into the woods, and stood over the top of me with her front claws digging into either shoulder, and her head directly over mine. That's when she cocked her head sideways and bit down across my face. I was in a medically induced coma for those first 12 days. The medical report put it this way: “Patient arrived at the hospital in a condition incompatible with life.” I’ll never forget that first time when your mom came into the hospital room. I couldn't talk, you know, and so, I wrote down on a whiteboard, “I'm blind.” And she's like, “Yeah, I know.” And I wrote down, “I'm scared.” I didn't think I was gonna be able to have love or have kids. Acacia Bigley: But why did that make you think you couldn't be a father? Dan Bigley: Well, you know me, I always like to joke that I was the first blind person I ever met. [Laughs] Dan Bigley: And so, I had this fear, like, how does a blind guy change diapers? How do I make sure I don't knock my toddler down the stairs? You know, your mom and I had a really tough time. I kind of pushed her away, and she was pretty sad and mad. But I realized that I was stuck in a place of bitterness… and a life of bitterness had more ability to destroy what life I had left than the bear did. Acacia Bigley: Mm-hmm. Dan Bigley: I called your mom and said sorry. And… Acacia Bigley: And that's how I’m here today? Dan Bigley: Thank goodness. Acacia Bigley: I know. When I was little, I just knew that there was a lot more things that I had to help you with than other kids, and I thought other parents were different, and you were the only normal one. [Laughs] Dan Bigley: I remember when you and your brother were really little, and you guys would have on your little monkey backpacks with the tails. I would use you guys as my guides holding onto your monkey tails. Acacia Bigley: We were your guide dogs. Dan Bigley: Uh-huh, my guide monkeys. Dan Bigley: One night, we were just sitting there in your bed, and you were getting ready to go to sleep, and you just said to me, “Dad, are you happy?” And I said, “Yeah, I'm super happy.” A moment or two later you said… “Sooooo you're blind and you're happy?” [Laughs] I was like, “Yeah, I'm blind and I'm happy.” [Text] Listen. On the morning of April 19, 1995, a truck bomb exploded outside the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in downtown Oklahoma City, killing 168 people and injuring hundreds more. It was the deadliest act of homegrown terrorism in United States history—a moment that shattered lives and forever changed a city. As we mark the 30th anniversary on April 19, 2025, we remember each life lost and honor the families, survivors, and first responders who lived through the unthinkable. Thirty years later, the stories of courage, heartbreak, and resilience still echo—across Oklahoma and throughout the nation.
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] On the morning of April 19, 1995, a truck bomb exploded at the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City. It killed 168 people and injured hundreds more, making it the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in U.S. History. The federal office building housed a day care center, and the truck packed with explosives was parked directly beneath it. Of the 21 children who were there that morning, only six survived. Christopher Nguyen was 4 years old and enrolled at the daycare center. At StoryCorps, he and his mother, Phuong Nguyen, talk about the lasting impact of that day. Phuong Nguyen (PN): I remember that day clearly, even twenty years later. I was sitting in office, and there goes “BOOM!" My boss come over and say, "It is the Federal Building. Did you have your baby at the day care there?" I say, "Oh my god." You was the third child brought out, you have bleeding from the head down through your face And you were screaming and crying like crazy. Chris Nguyen (CN): A lot of times people ask me, "What do you remember?" But, I don't remember anything. PN: On the anniversary, we used to hide the newspaper. We turn off the TV. We don't want you to see, to hear. CN: And then I found out in kindergarten. Some girl brought in a clip for show-and-tell. It was the bombing, and I started crying. That's the first time I heard about it, but I knew it was the bombing. Nobody had to say it to me. I already knew. PN: That day, it left a scar in our life. And you know scar, it going to stay with you. It's not going to go away. CN: There are stories, there are interviews, there are news reports every year, uh, that tell me exactly what happened, and, apparently, I'm a part of it. But you remember the Harry Potter movies? PN: Mmm-hmm. CN: In the story, his parents die, and he survives somehow. And he doesn't know why, and he doesn't remember because he was also a baby. That is what it's like for me. I guess I've never really talked to you and Dad about this… there's a lot of pressure to make both of you proud, but also for all the parents who lost their own children. They won't ever get to have that sense of pride when they see their own children succeeding. And when I'm thinking about what I'm doing with my life, I have to think about all of the children that were in that day care that day, and how I'm lucky to have survived. I wouldn't want to waste this opportunity that they don't have. [Text] PJ Allen was one year old at the time of the bombing. He suffered broken bones, severe burns, and damage to his lungs from inhaling debris. At StoryCorps in Oklahoma City, he spoke with his father, Willie Watson. Willie Watson (WW): We were in that hospital for three months. But I think it was about two or three weeks before you even woke up. PJ Allen (PA): I never really fully understood, what happened or even what I was part of. As far as I knew, I was a normal kid. WW: After all these years, 20 years, this is the first time we've sat down and actually talked about the bombing. I wanted to protect you. And I never wanted to relive it with you. Because, I personally hold myself responsible for you getting hurt. I was supposed to take you to the daycare that day. But that morning when your mom was getting ready to go to work, she asked me, did, did I want her to take you. And I told her, I said, “Well hey, you know, I’m pretty tired. I’m going to sleep another 30 minutes or so, so go ahead and take him." But, if I would have kept you there with me, you wouldn’t have got to the federal building until the bombing would have been over. You wouldn't have even been there. PA: I never knew that you had blamed yourself for what had happened to me that day. WW: Sometimes I'll be sleeping, I'll just be in a cold sweat. And I'll wake up because of the nightmares I have. PA: I don’t want you to walk around with this burden I want you to be alive inside. I'm never angry about my situation. I’m alright, I’m good. I like so many things about you, Dad. You're always the coolest guy in the room. I'm like, “Alright, when I get to that age, I'm be just like him. Walk in, be the man.” And, I don’t hold you responsible for that day in any way. WW: I still wrestle with it, but, you were the one that was in there. And to see you come back was a miracle, and I’m proud of you. And I love you. PA: I wouldn’t trade that for anything else in the world. I love you very much, and I’m glad that you’re my dad. [Text] Listen. Honor. Share. Patrice Hudson wasn’t sure online dating was for her — until she met Byron Ball, a fellow single parent and former spouse who taught high school science. He had a passion for gardening and poured that love into the yard outside her home, which she had no time for. At StoryCorps, she reflected on the quiet legacy he left behind — and how it continues to remind her that love never truly disappears.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en In his profile, we kind of had a dad bod, but I have a mom bod. And when you look deeper in the eyes behind the expression, that's where the handsome is. He had the warmest smile and really beautiful eyes. And he was very handsome. We talked every night on the phone. He was funny and sensitive. and he loved gardening. As a single mom, I did not have time for gardening. I think it pained him to see the status of my backyard. He was very kind about it. He never criticized me, but he did ask if he could plant things for me. Over time, he did a little more and more in the yard to make it pretty. He often did things to show he cared without being asked. But he was diagnosed with cancer eight years after we met. We married in his backyard garden. And about 9 weeks after we married, he passed away. That winter, the house felt big and empty. You know, I didn't feel much like Thanksgiving. I didn't want a Christmas tree. That year felt gray and somber. That spring one morning I realized, "Oh, there were little tulips popping up in a corner of my yard. They were a very rich, lovely purple." Byron knew that purple was my favorite color, so he planted those flowers. He knew he wouldn't live to see them bloom. I could not hold in the tears because with every ounce of my being, I knew that I was loved. That it didn't die with him. He wanted me to know that I did take up gardening. When I'm in the garden, I have had a few tears, but mostly it's joyful. I think that's what Byron would have wanted. He understood that life goes on without him and that's okay. And I knew that if she was alive, the first thing she'd do would be call Dad. And so I stayed by the telephone, but of course I never received the call… I was so full of revenge and hate, I didn't even want a trial for Tim McVay or Terry Nichols. I remember I went to the bomb site every single day after her death. And, I was across the street from the Murrah building. My head was splitting, because I started, uh, self-medicating with alcohol after Julie's death. And that afternoon, I asked myself what did I need to do to be able to move forward. And I finally came to the conclusion, for me personally, that the day that we would take Tim McVey or Terry Nichols to kill them was not gonna be part of my healing process. After I got that settled in my mind, I was able to stop the drinking, stop smoking, and I never want to go through another year like that in my life. That's the most miserable time I ever spent. And, I had seen Bill McVay, the father of Tim McVay, on television. And I don't recall a single question that that reporter asked that day, but on his final answer, he looked directly into the lens of the television camera for just a couple of seconds. When he did that, I could see this deep pain in his eye, and I recognized that pain immediately. And I knew that someday I needed to go tell that man that I did not blame him or his family for what his son had done. And nearly three and a half years later, I had the opportunity to do that. When I finally went through that process, all of a sudden it was like this tremendous weight had been removed from my shoulders. And I honestly have never felt closer to God than I did at that moment. I was able to start feeling a little bit of peace. And I say that in spite of the fact I no longer have Julie. When your parents die, you go to the hilltop and you bury them. When your children die, you bury them in your heart, and it's forever. It's difficult for me to imagine what Julie would be like today, because to me, Julie will always be 23 years old. That's burned in my mind. She'll always be 23 to me. [Text] Listen. Honor. Share. Dan Bigley’s life changed in 2003 when he was mauled by a grizzly bear while fishing on Alaska’s Kenai River. He survived the attack but woke from a 12-day coma to find he had lost his sight. The outdoor activities that once shaped his life were no longer possible, and he faced uncertainty about his future—whether he’d find fulfilling work, build relationships, or have a family. At StoryCorps, Dan spoke with his daughter, Acacia, about how he learned to imagine a new future for himself.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] Fifteen year old Acacia Bigley brought her father Dan to StoryCorps in Anchorage, Alaska to hear how he became blind. Before Acacia was born, Dan was on a fishing trip when he was attacked by a grizzly bear after he accidentally came between her and her cubs. Dan Bigley: She drug me off into the woods, and stood over the top of me with her front claws digging into either shoulder, and her head directly over mine. That's when she cocked her head sideways and bit down across my face. I was in a medically induced coma for those first 12 days. The medical report put it this way: “Patient arrived at the hospital in a condition incompatible with life.” I’ll never forget that first time when your mom came into the hospital room. I couldn't talk, you know, and so, I wrote down on a whiteboard, “I'm blind.” And she's like, “Yeah, I know.” And I wrote down, “I'm scared.” I didn't think I was gonna be able to have love or have kids. Acacia Bigley: But why did that make you think you couldn't be a father? Dan Bigley: Well, you know me, I always like to joke that I was the first blind person I ever met. [Laughs] Dan Bigley: And so, I had this fear, like, how does a blind guy change diapers? How do I make sure I don't knock my toddler down the stairs? You know, your mom and I had a really tough time. I kind of pushed her away, and she was pretty sad and mad. But I realized that I was stuck in a place of bitterness… and a life of bitterness had more ability to destroy what life I had left than the bear did. Acacia Bigley: Mm-hmm. Dan Bigley: I called your mom and said sorry. And… Acacia Bigley: And that's how I’m here today? Dan Bigley: Thank goodness. Acacia Bigley: I know. On the morning of April 19, 1995, a truck bomb exploded outside the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in downtown Oklahoma City, killing 168 people and injuring hundreds more. It was the deadliest act of homegrown terrorism in United States history—a moment that shattered lives and forever changed a city. As we mark the 30th anniversary on April 19, 2025, we remember each life lost and honor the families, survivors, and first responders who lived through the unthinkable. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] On the morning of April 19, 1995, a truck bomb exploded at the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City. It killed 168 people and injured hundreds more, making it the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in U.S. History. The federal office building housed a day care center, and the truck packed with explosives was parked directly beneath it. Of the 21 children who were there that morning, only six survived. Christopher Nguyen was 4 years old and enrolled at the daycare center. At StoryCorps, he and his mother, Phuong Nguyen, talk about the lasting impact of that day. Phuong Nguyen (PN): I remember that day clearly, even twenty years later. I was sitting in office, and there goes “BOOM!" My boss come over and say, "It is the Federal Building. Did you have your baby at the day care there?" I say, "Oh my god." You was the third child brought out, you have bleeding from the head down through your face And you were screaming and crying like crazy. Chris Nguyen (CN): A lot of times people ask me, "What do you remember?" But, I don't remember anything. PN: On the anniversary, we used to hide the newspaper. We turn off the TV. We don't want you to see, to hear. CN: And then I found out in kindergarten. Some girl brought in a clip for show-and-tell. It was the bombing, and I started crying. That's the first time I heard about it, but I knew it was the bombing. Nobody had to say it to me. I already knew. PN: That day, it left a scar in our life. And you know scar, it going to stay with you. It's not going to go away. CN: There are stories, there are interviews, there are news reports every year, uh, that tell me exactly what happened, and, apparently, I'm a part of it. But you remember the Harry Potter movies? PN: Mmm-hmm. CN: In the story, his parents die, and he survives somehow. And he doesn't know why, and he doesn't remember because he was also a baby. That is what it's like for me. I guess I've never really talked to you and Dad about this… there's a lot of pressure to make both of you proud, but also for all the parents who lost their own children. They won't ever get to have that sense of pride when they see their own children succeeding. And when I'm thinking about what I'm doing with my life, I have to think about all of the children that were in that day care that day, and how I'm lucky to have survived. I wouldn't want to waste this opportunity that they don't have. [Text] PJ Allen was one year old at the time of the bombing. He suffered broken bones, severe burns, and damage to his lungs from inhaling debris. At StoryCorps in Oklahoma City, he spoke with his father, Willie Watson. Willie Watson (WW): We were in that hospital for three months. But I think it was about two or three weeks before you even woke up. PJ Allen (PA): I never really fully understood, what happened or even what I was part of. As far as I knew, I was a normal kid. WW: After all these years, 20 years, this is the first time we've sat down and actually talked about the bombing. I wanted to protect you. And I never wanted to relive it with you. Because, I personally hold myself responsible for you getting hurt. I was supposed to take you to the daycare that day. But that morning when your mom was getting ready to go to work, she asked me, did, did I want her to take you. And I told her, I said, “Well hey, you know, I’m pretty tired. I’m going to sleep another 30 minutes or so, so go ahead and take him." But, if I would have kept you there with me, you wouldn’t have got to the federal building until the bombing would have been over. You wouldn't have even been there. PA: I never knew that you had blamed yourself for what had happened to me that day. WW: Sometimes I'll be sleeping, I'll just be in a cold sweat. And I'll wake up because of the nightmares I have. PA: I don’t want you to walk around with this burden I want you to be alive inside. I'm never angry about my situation. I’m alright, I’m good. I like so many things about you, Dad. You're always the coolest guy in the room. I'm like, “Alright, when I get to that age, I'm be just like him. Walk in, be the man.” And, I don’t hold you responsible for that day in any way. WW: I still wrestle with it, but, you were the one that was in there. And to see you come back was a miracle, and I’m proud of you. And I love you. PA: I wouldn’t trade that for anything else in the world. I love you very much, and I’m glad that you’re my dad. [Text] Listen. Honor. Share. Palacio wrote White Bird: A Wonder Story, to show how love, courage, and kindness had the power to save lives during the Holocaust. The graphic novel was adapted into a film by acclaimed director Marc Forster. At StoryCorps, R.J, and Marc sat down to talk about how White Bird's theme of kindness has impacted their lives, and their hopes that the film inspires audiences to #BeBrave and #ChooseKind. Marc: When I read White Bird, to be honest, I felt like this is a story very different than other Holocaust stories and something I haven't seen before. R.J.: Yeah, you know, the idea behind White Bird really is to show how genocide starts with the ostracizing of groups of people. It starts with hate speech and the normalizing of hate speech. But I also wanted to talk about how kindness, or one act of kindness, can really alter the course of someone's life, and actually has. One of the most wonderful things about real history is there are an abundance of stories about people sticking their neck out for people they didn't know. You know, I'd like to think that I'd be that person, but I think kindness is really hard. And we underestimate how hard it is. You actually have to choose to be kind. Marc: Yes, the courage it takes to be kind. I'm always inspired about people who have the courageousness to stand up for humanity. I mean, in my life, you know, I had a few mentors who who were very kind to me. And one in specific was a man called Robert Louis-Dreyfus You know, I grew up in Switzerland in the mountains And then when I finished high school, I applied to all sorts of film school around the world. I got into NYU and my parents didn't have the financial backing to pay to go to school in the States. And Robert said, "Look, I will finance your studies." And then when I had the money to pay him back, he said, "No, just make great movies." I mean, I wouldn't be here if it wouldn't be for him. R.J.: That's an amazing story, and really, what a wonderful human being. There are a few people who I've met who are genuinely, instinctively kind. I can remember, we had just moved to a new building in Flushing, New York. We had just gone shopping. My mother had two large bags full of groceries and it was a third or fourth floor walk-up and she dropped both grocery bags. I remember the sound of the milk in a glass bottle on the marble landing of the staircase and she was in the verge of tears. The neighbor, a woman named Alice, she saw what had just happened and she came out with a broom and a mop to help my mother sweep up. And it was an act of kindness that I remember had such an impact on me as a five-year-old, watching my mother having a terrible day, I think kindness lifts people up and it kind of raises the bar on our expectations of one another. You can't really mandate kindness, but you can inspire it. And my hope is that if you inspire it in enough people, it becomes the norm. Marc: Yeah, if we can manage that, that's really a lot, because I believe in humanity. I'm an optimist. I always think I have to see the light at the end of the tunnel. When I first started to make movies, I realized how movies actually can affect society and how much they can help people or inspire them. R.J.: Yeah, you know, I think, your movies, certainly White Bird, is all about ordinary people living in extraordinary times, doing the best they can with what they have, finding that hero inside of them to do what's right. So, the more we can talk about and celebrate people like that, you know we can appeal to our better angels and inspire people to want to be better. So, I think we're doing really good work, Marc. And she said, "Well,  honey, Mommy passed away this morning." And I remember at my mother's wake,   someone in my family came to me and  said, "Johnny, your teacher's here." Cecile Doyle: When I found out she died, I could  certainly relate to that, because when I was 11,   my own father died. And you just don't know  how you're going to go on without that person. JC: When I returned to school,   you waited until the other children  left the room at the end of the day,   and you told me that you were there if I needed you. And you bent over and kissed me on the head. It was really the only time someone said to me,   "I know what you're feeling,  and I know what you're missing." And I felt, in a very real way,  that things really would be okay. CD: Well, John, I really loved you as a student,   and I'm so glad that I could be  there with you for that time. JC: Many years later, when I became a teacher,   I started to think more and more about you.  And I started to think to myself, "Here I am,   with a memory of a teacher who changed  my life, and I've never told her that." My name is John Cruitt, and I was in your  third grade class during the 1958-1959 school year. Two days before Christmas, my  mother passed away, and you told me that   you were there if I needed you. I hope life  has been as kind to you as you were to me. God bless you, always. With great fondness, John. CD: And your letter could not have come at a  better time because my husband had Parkinson's,   and he was going downhill. And I had  just come home from the hospital,   and I read this beautiful letter,  and I just was overwhelmed. JC: Well the funny thing is when I finally  wrote to you again after 54 years, I typed   the letter--I was afraid my penmanship  wasn't going to meet your standards! JC: Well, after all this time Mrs.  Doyle, all I can say to you is: thank you. CD: John, what can I say, I'm just glad that  we made a difference in each other's life.

Miss Indian World is the most prestigious Indigenous pageant in North America, where young women are judged on categories ranging from traditional dance and talent to public speaking and tribal knowledge. The winner spends the next year as a Native ambassador, traveling across the continent and around the world to meet with tribal communities. Lillian Sparks Robinson won the pageant in 2000, and using what she learned during her reign, went on to serve as the Commissioner for the Administration for Native Americans under President Obama. She came to StoryCorps with her mom, Georgeline Sparks, to remember winning the competition.

Listen to their story in honor of #IndigenousPeoplesDay.
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US Senator Byron L. Dorgan: Ms. Sparks, welcome to the Committee. My understanding is you are accompanied by your mother. Is that correct? Would you wish to introduce her to us? Lillian Sparks Robinson: It would be my honor to introduce her. My mother, Georgeline Brushbreaker Sparks, Oyate Waha Canka YaPi Win, Shield For Her People Woman, is accompanying me today. Byron: Well, we welcome her. Lillian: The last day of the competition. I just remember you sitting at the sewing machine... 5 o'clock in the morning... Putting final touches on my dress and my beadwork. You were sewing a zipper and you sewed it upside down at first. And oh, my God. You were upset and frustrated. You took those seam rippers and just ripped that zipper out quick and you pricked your finger. So there was a drop of blood on my legging. And I remember thinking, “Wow, there's literal blood, sweat, and tears, sewn into my outfit, getting me ready for this moment. Georgeline Sparks: I remember you being so calm and me being a bundle of nerves. And that's how I like it to be, for me to take on that extra burden. I think that's kind of a mom trait, though. Lillian: When Miss Indian World is crowned, it's very dramatic, you know, they dim the lights, and there's a spotlight. And when they said, “From the Rosebud Sioux Tribe, contestant number five, Lillian Sparks,” it wasn't until I saw you that I became emotional.

Miss Indian World is the most prestigious Indigenous pageant in North America, where young women are judged on categories ranging from traditional dance and talent to public speaking and tribal knowledge. The winner spends the next year as a Native ambassador, traveling across the continent and around the world to meet with tribal communities. Lillian Sparks Robinson won the pageant in 2000, and using what she learned during her reign, went on to serve as the Commissioner for the Administration for Native Americans under President Obama. She came to StoryCorps with her mom, Georgeline Sparks, to remember winning the competition.

Listen to their story in honor of #IndigenousPeoplesDay.

My mother, Georgeline Brushbreaker Sparks, Oyate Waha Canka YaPi Win, Shield For Her People Woman, is accompanying me today. Byron: Well, we welcome her. Lillian: The last day of the competition. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US Jean Kanokogi: Her first judo tournament was in 1959 It was the YMCA Judo Championships in Utica, New York. Women weren't allowed to compete back then. So, she went with the men that she was training with just to warm up with them. But then she heard a snap and a loud yell across the mat. It was one of her teammates. Her coach said, “Rusty, I need you to take the place of this teammate. He can’t compete. Otherwise we’ll forfeit. But don't let anybody see that you're a woman. Just make it a tie. She was big and strong, she was very androgynous looking, so nobody really knew the difference. She bows in with her opponent. She throws this big guy and wins her judo match. As she's walking out of the judo venue with her gold medal, the tournament director comes up to her and says, “Are you a girl? I need that medal back. Otherwise, your team will forfeit their first place win.” So she decided to take that medal from around her neck. And she told me that she felt that she did everything wrong just for being a woman. But then she also described that she felt this anger that she never felt before. She didn't believe that any woman deserved to have that feeling because they wanted to compete.

In 1964, civil rights groups organized Freedom Schools across the state of Mississippi, drawing over 2,500 children to 41 schools for lessons that ranged from literature and math to government and civic engagement. Many teachers were white college students from across the country. Hattiesburg led with six schools, the most of any town. This was part of the larger program called, “Freedom Summer,” where over 700 volunteers aimed to register Black voters and fight discrimination. Sixty years later, former students Deborah Carr, Stephanie Hoze, Theresia Clark-Banks, Julia Clark-Ward, Glenda Funchess, and Don Denard reflect on that summer. As heard on NPR's "Morning Edition" on Friday, July 26th, 2024. 

Learn more: https://storycorps.org/stories/sixty-years-later-the-children-of-freedom-summer-look-back/

Alton Russell was the long-time Chair of the Republican party in Columbus, Georgia. Wane Hailes was the head of the local NAACP chapter. Although they knew of each other, they had never actually spoken—until they sat down for this One Small Step conversation.

One Small Step brings strangers with different political views together to record a 50-minute conversation—not to debate politics, but to learn more about who we are as people. Learn more: takeonesmallstep.org

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en [Text]: Alton Russell is the former Chair of the Republican Party in Columbus, Georgia. Wane Hailes is President of the local chapter of the NAACP. They knew of each other, but had never spoken. Until now... Alton: I went looking for a job, and there was a guy sitting at the desk. He said, "What will you do?" And I said, "Anything as long as it's legal." He says, "Good answer." By the way my name is George Bush. It was George H.W. Bush! Wane: Really? Alton: Yes, sir. And he was running for Congress. What my job was is I made yard signs. Wane: But you never run for office? Alton: No, never have. Wane: You've just been the kingmaker. Alton: Well, I don't know about that, but I'm, no, I never have run. Wane: What do you do for a living? Alton: Believe it or not, I'm a toilet paper salesman. Wane: Really? Alto: Yes, sir. Wane: Two ply? Alton: Two ply, wiping it up, yeah. I've been there 40 years. Wane: Is that right? Alton: Yeah. But I just wonder, how in the world did you wind up in Columbus, Georgia? Did you take a wrong turn? Wane: I was working for the YMCA, and the YMCA here called and said, would I be interested? But, as the president of the NAACP, I can tell you how I got into that. When we were growing up, about eight or nine years old, we were traveling to my grandfather's house, and we stopped at a laundromat. They said, “We don't wash Black folks clothes here.” Of course, they didn't use the “Black folks” word... My father being a preacher, you know, he was cool, but my mother was ready to go off. You know, and we went on to my grandfather's house, and he called the NAACP. They said, “Go on back up to the laundromat.” And the white owner stood in the corner while we washed our clothes, red as a beet. In 1964, civil rights groups organized Freedom Schools across the state of Mississippi, drawing over 2,500 children to 41 schools for lessons that ranged from literature and math to government and civic engagement. Many teachers were white college students from across the country. Hattiesburg led with six schools, the most of any town. This was part of the larger program called, “Freedom Summer,” where over 700 volunteers aimed to register Black voters and fight discrimination. Sixty years later, former students Deborah Carr, Stephanie Hoze, Theresia Clark-Banks, Julia Clark-Ward, Glenda Funchess, and Don Denard reflect on that summer. As heard on NPR's "Morning Edition" on Friday, July 26th, 2024. 

Learn more: https://storycorps.org/stories/sixty-years-later-the-children-of-freedom-summer-look-back/

Growing up in 1950s suburban St. Louis, Missouri, Judd Esty-Kendall remembers a childhood surrounded by animals. His father, Henry, a salesman and WWII veteran, cared for farm animals and a variety of wild ones, including a wolf named Peter. At StoryCorps, Judd shares a conversation with his son, also named Jud, recalling the special bond shared between Henry and Peter. Originally aired April 5, 2024, on NPR’s Morning Edition.

https://storycorps.org/stories/the-wolf-was-his-best-friend-remembering-henry-kendall/
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en-US [Text] Growing up in St. Louis during the 1950s, Judd Esty-Kendall Sr. remembers growing up with falcons, raccoons, even a flying squirrel. They belonged to his father, Henry, a salesman and World War veteran who took in wild animals in his spare time. At StoryCorps, Judd told his own son about a special bond between one animal and his dad. Judd Esty-Kendall (JEK Sr.): We got a full-blooded wolf as a young pup. It was named Peter. We would all take turns giving the wolf a bottle and it grew up beautiful, strong, intelligent. My father would come home in his suit from the city after working all day, strip into old clothes and go out in the backyard and wrestle with the wolf. But, I cannot remember any times when he came home and did anything with the kids and the family. Jud Esty-Kendall (JEK Jr.): Do you think his military service had anything to do with that? JEK Sr: Yeah. World War II totally changed his life, because he suffered from fairly serious PTSD, untreated. And he was really very nervous about being with people. The wolf was his best friend. It was his way of having a bond with a living being that did not make him anxious. But then, Peter scared the bejesus out of some neighborhood kids who came onto our property.
